articles.title: New Facility Brings Off-Highway Wet Friction Production to India

paras.en: New Facility Brings Off-Highway Wet Friction Production to India

Carlisle Brake & Friction has broken ground to expand its Chennai, India manufacturing operations in one of the world’s fastest-growing industrial regions. Having produced mechatronic products in the region for more than 15 years, Carlisle CBF will relocate to add production at a larger site for off-highway paper wet friction discs and steel separator plates. The new facility is scheduled to open in 2027.

The move to expanded space is designed to accommodate manufacturing capabilities needed to serve the growing demand across the agriculture, construction and especially mining industries in India and Southeast Asia. Local production will improve supply chain responsiveness while supporting original equipment and aftermarket requirements in cost-sensitive markets.

Carlisle Brake & Friction is establishing a state-of-the-art wet friction manufacturing facility on par with proven global manufacturing processes in the new Chennai plant, to build a more resilient regional platform. This expansion strengthens our ability to deliver durable wet friction products that help keep critical off-highway equipment productive.

articles.title: Mitchell, Tractable to Transform Collision Intake Through Automated Vehicle Inspection and Estimating
articles.author: Jason Stahl

paras.en: Mitchell announced plans to expand its collaboration with Tractable through a proposed, exclusive agreement focused on optimizing the vehicle intake process. By connecting Tractable’s LumaScanner vehicle inspection system with Mitchell’s automated estimating solution, Mitchell Intelligent Estimating, the companies intend to help North American multi-site operators and independent collision repair centers accelerate damage assessment and preliminary estimate creation.

“Every decision about a vehicle, whether to service it, repair it or sell it, depends on knowing its true condition,” said Venkat Sathyamurthy, CEO of Tractable. “Our ambition for LumaScanner is to make that knowledge available to everyone who relies on it, anytime, anywhere. Integrating LumaScanner with Mitchell’s intelligent solutions will bring that vision into the heart of collision repair, extending the value of the inspection into the estimating process itself.”

As a vehicle passes through, LumaScanner automatically inspects it and produces a condition report: a consistent, time-stamped record of the vehicle’s physical state. Once integrated with Mitchell’s cloud ecosystem, that condition report could feed Mitchell Intelligent Estimating to automatically generate a preliminary estimate for appraisers to review and edit.

Together with Mitchell’s existing mobile photo-capture capabilities, the planned offering would give repairers the flexibility to document vehicle damage through either a physical or digital intake process. In AI estimating, capturing high-quality images of the damaged vehicle increases the accuracy and completeness of the preliminary estimate.

With LumaScanner, the vehicle is driven or towed through the inspection system and the vehicle image set and condition report will be used to generate a preliminary estimate in minutes. This is designed to save time and assist in improving estimate accuracy and completeness.

“Our goal is to help collision repairers simplify the vehicle intake process by connecting innovative technologies that are designed to optimize key steps in the workflow,” said Olivier Baudoux, senior vice president of global product strategy and artificial intelligence at Mitchell. “Combining LumaScanner’s automated inspection capabilities with Mitchell’s advanced solutions, proprietary data and open, cloud-based platform is intended to give repairers a way to remove friction, improve productivity and safely return collision-damaged vehicles to the road.”

articles.title: SEMA Show Spotlights AI Repair Tools, ADAS Calibration and More
articles.author: Jason Stahl

paras.en: The 2026 SEMA Show concluded four days at the Las Vegas Convention Center, bringing together more than 150,000 industry professionals, media and enthusiasts from 140 countries and more than 2,200 exhibiting brands, including 400 first-time exhibitors.

The event served as a global marketplace for the automotive aftermarket, an industry that generates $383 billion in annual economic impact, supports 1.25 million jobs and produces $107.7 billion in wages nationwide. Across the show campus, manufacturers, buyers, builders, educators and media connected around products, technologies and relationships driving the market forward.

“The SEMA Show reflects the scale, creativity and economic importance of the automotive aftermarket,” said Mike Spagnola, CEO of SEMA. “This year’s event built on that foundation with an expanded powersports and motorcycle presence, advancements in emerging propulsion technologies, automation and smart manufacturing, and new opportunities to connect with consumers. Those developments underscore the strength of the market and the opportunities emerging across the industry.”
New Products Translate Technology into Practical Solutions

The 2026 SEMA Show highlighted an automotive aftermarket focused on turning emerging technologies into practical, market-ready solutions. Thousands of products were entered in the New Products Showcase and debuted across the show floor, reflecting advances in AI-enabled repair tools, ADAS calibration equipment, connected technology and performance components.

Key trends included the growing use of AI to streamline repair procedures and shop operations; greater integration of technology, durability and functionality into truck, off-road and powersports products; and continued improvements in performance and comfort for classic vehicles.
Automakers Use SEMA as a Launch Platform
Major automakers and performance organizations participated throughout the week, reinforcing the show’s role as a global meeting place where OEMs and aftermarket innovation intersect.
- Ford Motor Company unveiled a ’66 Ford Racing R125 Mustang Fastback, a heritage-inspired vehicle built with Ford Racing parts to mark the organization’s 125th anniversary.

- Honda Racing Corp. (Honda/Acura) showcased the recently unveiled Passport Baja Spec Trophy Truck, Passport TrailSport Baja Chase and HRC Performance Parts for the Civic Type R, Integra Type S and Passport TrailSport.
- Mitsubishi unveiled its 2028 Outlander Diamond Trail Edition in a global debut.
- Nissan unveiled new Frontier, Pathfinder and Armada concepts, along with a Sentra Spec-V and two enthusiast-inspired Z concepts.

- Stellantis, through Dodge, Jeep and Mopar, unveiled its Jeep Wrangler Scrambler SRT Concept, showcased its Jeep Wrangler BUZZCUT concept and introduced an all-new series of crate engine packages through Direct Connection, the factory-backed performance arm of Stellantis’ SRT performance division.
- Toyota introduced its Snowhunter Concept lineup, featuring the Tundra, Tacoma, 4Runner, Land Cruiser and Sequoia.
Expanded Powersports Section Broadens Business Opportunities

The expanded Powersports, Side-by-Side (SxS) and Adventure Lifestyle section featured dirt bikes, motorcycles, side-by-sides, trailers, tow vehicles, gear and adventure-lifestyle products. The section brought together brands and industry organizations, including Harley-Davidson, Kawasaki Motors Corp., Yamaha Watercraft, Kymco USA Inc., Inferno Eyewear, Denago, Shock Therapy and the National Powersports Dealers Association.

Its placement gave attendees opportunities to explore new business categories while providing a high-visibility platform for exhibitors such as Massimo Motor, a manufacturer and distributor of powersports vehicles, UTVs, ATVs and mobility solutions.

“We’re really excited to be here because we launched the Sentinel 1500, as well as the Warrior 1500,” said Ron Luttrell, vice president of dealer development for Massimo Motor. “It was the first time the public had seen them, so launching at SEMA was important to us. The feedback has been overwhelmingly positive for both of those units, the brand and the other units we displayed.”

SEMA Battle of the Builders Presented by Mothers expanded in 2026 with the addition of the Bike Builder Shootout, recognizing standout motorcycle builds. More than 50 motorcycles were entered into the competition with Steven Iacona earning the inaugural championship for his customized Harley Davidson Knucklehead.

“I am truly grateful for this honor,” said Iacona. “The entire event was incredible. The competition was difficult, but I will absolutely be back next year. Thank you to everyone at SEMA for inviting custom bike builders to participate. It was amazing.”
Developing the Next Generation of Skilled Professionals

Preparing the next generation of industry talent was another theme of the 2026 SEMA Show, with hands-on experiences and education connecting students with career opportunities in the automotive aftermarket.

In the inaugural Ford Custom Garage Ultimate Build Competition, six Washtenaw Community College students brought an attendee-designed Ford Bronco to life, building the vehicle live in the Ford booth before its Friday reveal.

The SEMA Show Student Program reached a milestone, attracting more than 1,000 students, an all-time high. Education sessions highlighted workforce development strategies and ways companies can connect with emerging talent and recruit future employees.
The program was part of SEMA Education, which featured education sessions across multiple SEMA-led and partner tracks.
Eddie Pettus won the 2026 SEMA Battle of the Builders Presented by Mothers competition with his ’70 Chevrolet Chevelle.

Thomas Kincer of Kincer Chassis won the 2026 SEMA Best Engineered Vehicle of the Year Award for his ’77 Ford F-100. The annual award recognizes a feature vehicle at the SEMA Show that demonstrates exceptional engineering.
Friday Expands Industry-Consumer Connection

On Nov. 6, SEMA Show Friday — Open to the Public welcomed enthusiasts to experience the exhibit halls, vehicle builds and demonstrations. The SEMA Cruise carried show vehicles out of the convention center, while SEMA Fest continued the celebration with performances by The Offspring, Jimmy Eat World, 311 and The Alive.

SEMA Live presented by AutoZone delivered 32 hours of scheduled coverage from the show campus on SEMA’s YouTube and Facebook channels. Coverage included product and vehicle reveals, interviews, outdoor demonstrations, Battle of the Builders and the SEMA Cruise. Highlights and on-demand coverage from the 2026 event are available through SEMA’s YouTube and Facebook channels.

As a catalyst for commerce across the aftermarket, the SEMA Show connects the people, products and ideas that help businesses grow and the industry prosper. The show returns to Las Vegas Nov. 2-5, 2027 for its 60th anniversary, and exhibitors are encouraged to plan early: the priority booth-space application deadline has moved up to Feb. 1, 2027.
Visit semashow.com for more information.

articles.title: South Carolina’s governor-elect holds first press conference at auto body shop
articles.author: Teresa Moss

paras.en: Alan Wilson, South Carolina’s next governor, held his first press conference after the mid-term election at a West Columbia body shop where he worked his first job at 15, according to local media.
The governor-elect said he worked at Reeley’s Auto Body shop as a car washer.
He told the media that the shop is symbolic.
“A shop like this is where you come to fix a car, repair a car, improve a car, and that’s really what this transition is about,” News19 reports Wilson as saying.
He said his transition into the role is repairing and improving a governmental system that is “broken or damaged.”
Wilson, current Attorney General, said an audit of the state’s government will be his first course of action. This will include a public website that publishes government data for the general public.
He also said he will ask lawmakers to give the governor the power to temporarily suspend the gas tax during price spikes. He added that the neighboring Georgia governor has this authority.
“I also understand that we rely on the gas tax to fund infrastructure projects and road construction,” News19 reports Wilson as saying. He adds that the power will need guardrails.
Improving roads and bridges has been a part of Wilson’s campaign platform.

“As part of his Families First Audit Initiative, he will modernize the Department of Transportation, demand transparency, streamline project timelines, and make sure every region of the state benefits from long-overdue improvements,” Wilson’s campaign website says. “Wilson understands rural communities have different infrastructure needs than urban communities. But we can’t prioritize one over the other–they both need attention.”

Fox Carolina previously reported that lowering insurance premiums is a part of Wilson’s plan. This includes reforming the Department of Insurance to allow for public audits of rate increases. He’d also required the department to give quarterly updates to the governor’s office and yearly reports on major carriers to the public.
South Carolina’s insurance commissioner position is appointed by the governor.

articles.title: Hyundai recalls vehicles for software malfunction that disables airbag
articles.author: Teresa Moss

paras.en: Hyundai has recalled 37,901 vehicles due to a software malfunction that disables the airbag, according to a National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) report.
The recall includes 2019-2022 Hyundai Veloster and 2019-2023 Hyundai Kona Electric models.

“The subject vehicles are equipped with an Airbag Control Unit (ACU) that detects crash signals and commands deployment of the airbag(s) and seat belt pretensioner(s),” the recall states. ”Under certain driving conditions, data may become corrupted during routine writing to the ACU’s memory, causing the airbag malfunction indicator light (MIL) to illuminate and the airbag system to deactivate.”
A deactivated airbag system may not deploy the vehicle’s airbags during a crash, increasing the risk of injury to vehicle occupants.
“A system reboot or power interruption while the ACU is writing data to its internal memory may result in data corruption,” the report states.
Hyundai started an investigation in August, 2024 after receiving an increase in airbag warning light warranty claims.

The automaker worked with ACU supplier ZF Group to conduct a series of technical reviews of recovered parts. The reviews included focusing on fault-detection conditions and proposed replication methods.
The two companies also performed electrical stress testing and held multiple vehicle-level replication tests in 2025.
By October 2026, Hyundai was updating its field data analysis and began finalizing its findings to date for review by its North America Safety Decision Authority (NASDA).
After reviewing the investigation findings, the company decided to conduct a safety recall, the report states.
As of November, Hyundai is aware of 331 unique incidents reported from October 2019 through September of this year.
The report adds that no crashes, fires, or injuries have been related to this condition.
Owners are instructed to bring their vehicle to a Hyundai dealer for an ACU software update. The remedy will be offered at no cost to owners for all affected vehicles.
NHTSA announced last week that it will invest $1.5 million to help states improve vehicle recall rates to keep roads safe.

“A vehicle with an open recall creates an avoidable hazard on our roads,” said NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison in a news release. “By giving states the resources to flag open recalls when drivers register or renew their vehicles, we can keep dangerous cars off our roads and American families safe.”
- “The development and execution of a reliable process to inform vehicle owners of any open safety recalls when registering their vehicles
- “Data-driven methods to measure recall completions
- “Comprehensive reports outlining the methodologies and processes used so best practices can be shared.”
Morrison announced the funding during a “Recalls Next: Technological Innovation & Safety Recalls” event.

NHTSA learned during the Takata airbag recalls that convincing consumers to remedy a recall is complicated, he said. Researchers found some consumers were confused about what the recall meant or simply didn’t remember receiving the notices.

“That’s troubling, because it means they didn’t necessarily ignore a serious warning,” Morrison said. “Some didn’t internalize the danger at all. The notices didn’t convey to them that a defective inflator could rupture and send metal shrapnel toward their faces—even when the notices literally said as much. It didn’t resonate that they – or someone they loved – could die if they didn’t act—even when informed through multiple channels.”

NHTSA oversaw nearly 900 vehicle safety recalls affecting more than 29 million vehicles last year. The agency’s data shows 3-year-old vehicles have an average completion rate of 68%, while 15-year-old vehicles have an 18% completion rate.
“Surveys tell us that about four in 10 owners named inconvenience as a main reason for not completing a recall,” Morrison said. “That should be taken seriously.”

State motor vehicle agencies have been effective partners in amplifying research messaging, he said. He added that during the Takata recall, DMV letters sometimes produced repair rates two to three times higher than manufacturer notices alone.
People recognize their DMV as an authoritative source of information that provides mail for critical transactional purposes linked to the ability to drive, Morrison said.

“If somebody sees the DMV logo on an official piece of mail and doesn’t open it, their driver’s license or vehicle registration might expire, which is connected to their ability to work, run errands, take care of family, and generally participate in society,” he explained. “Registration renewal creates a natural opportunity to reach an owner with information that matters.”

Morrison said NHTSA has also seen improvements in recall completions through other state avenues, such as Virginia’s EZPass toll collection system. The collaboration produced Takata recall completion rates eight to 10 times higher than comparable methods.
A collaboration with a vehicle auction company also resulted in repairs on about 90% of vehicles traded in with open recalls, he said.

NHTSA also recently launched a bulk VIN lookup tool that allows users to check up to 100 VINs at once for open safety recalls, making searches easier for dealerships, fleet operators and others managing multiple vehicles, Morrison said.
The agency has opened a public docket for feedback on recalls. Comments will be accepted here through Dec. 5.

articles.title: How It’s Made – and Why I Can’t Stop Watching
articles.author: Doug Kaufman

paras.en: I have a confession to make: I’m obsessed with How It’s Made.

If you’re unfamiliar with the TV series, it originally aired from 2001-2019, though it still lives on many different platforms. The show takes viewers inside factories and workshops to show how everyday products are manufactured. From tires and engine components to golf balls, pencils and potato chips, the show pulls back the curtain on the machines, materials and processes that make it all possible.
I’ve seen hundreds of episodes and I still can’t get enough of it. Like Zombieland, if How It’s Made is on TV, I’m stopping to watch.

My wife, on the other hand, does not share my enthusiasm. While I’m glued to the television watching a machine turn a chunk of metal into a precision component, she’s wondering how anyone could find this entertaining. I’ve tried explaining the appeal, but apparently watching 20 minutes of automated manufacturing isn’t her idea of a great evening.
What fascinates me isn’t just how things are made. It’s the fact that someone had to figure out how to make them in the first place.

Think about that for a moment. Somewhere along the line, someone looked at a problem, imagined a solution, designed a machine or process, tested it, made mistakes, adjusted the design and eventually figured out how to produce something consistently, efficiently and at scale.
Who thinks of this stuff? And how do they even begin?

I find that kind of ingenuity incredible. Even something as ordinary as a tire represents years of engineering, experimentation and refinement. The materials, tread design, manufacturing equipment and quality-control processes all exist because somebody asked a question and set out to find the answer.
That same curiosity belongs in the classroom and the service bay.

The best automotive technicians don’t just know how to replace a failed component. They want to understand why it failed, how it works and what the engineers were trying to accomplish when they designed it.
And that’s where instructors play such an important role.
Teaching a student how to perform a procedure is essential. But teaching that student to question, investigate and understand the reasoning behind the procedure is what builds a great technician.

When an instructor explains why a particular sensor works the way it does, why a diagnostic test matters or how a system’s components interact, they’re doing more than preparing students to pass a certification exam. They’re helping develop the curiosity and problem-solving skills that will carry those students through their careers.

Today’s students will spend their working lives servicing vehicles filled with technology that continues to evolve. Some may eventually become the engineers, designers or innovators who develop the next generation of automotive systems. Others will be the technicians who figure out how to diagnose and repair those systems when something doesn’t work as intended.
Either way, it starts with wanting to know how things work.

Maybe that’s why I find How It’s Made so entertaining. Every episode reminds me that behind even the simplest product is a series of questions, challenges and solutions. And behind those solutions are people who refused to stop asking, “What if we tried this?”
That’s the kind of thinking we should encourage in every automotive classroom.

As for my wife, I don’t expect her to join me for a marathon of industrial manufacturing anytime soon. But the next time an episode shows how an automotive component is made, I’ll probably call her into the room anyway.
Because seriously, how do people come up with this stuff?

articles.title: Arapahoe Community College Wins  AAPEX Engine Build
articles.author: Frank Strong

paras.en: A pair of high school students concurrently enrolled in automotive classes at Arapahoe Community College, won the 2026 AAPEX Student Competition. John Parmley, 16, and Schafer Eirich, 18, shaved more than an hour off the winning time from last year’s competition. The duo tore down and rebuilt a V8 engine in front of a live audience that was hundreds of people deep, in just 39 minutes and 11 seconds.

“It’s absolutely surreal,” said Eirich, following the competition. “We’ve been working toward this for so long; we saw it [the inaugural competition] last year and we knew in that moment we needed to do this.”

The competition tests the basic auto technician skills these students are learning. Each team starts with a small-block Chevy V8 engine and must dismantle the engine, including the pistons, crankshaft and camshaft. A judge then confirms the team has met the disassembly standard and the team races to rebuild it. The engine must turn when assembled; the fastest team wins.

“They’re amazing,” said Bob Parmley, the team’s coach and automotive instructor at the community college. “To build a champion team like this, it takes two guys who are willing to show up and work hard and take critical feedback.”

Through the generosity of aftermarket businesses that sponsored the event, the winning team took home an estimated $10,000 in prizes each. This included professional tool sets, which addresses one of the unique barriers for entry-level technicians and complicate the talent shortage: unlike other skilled trades, auto technicians must bring their own tools.

The Arapahoe team says they practiced two or three times a week for the last eight months. Finding time to practice was no small feat, given that both young men are in high school, taking college classes and also participating in school sports. However, busy schedules weren’t the only challenges the team faced.

First, John Parmley was hospitalized prior to the competition to have his appendix removed. He was unable to practice during the crucial week leading up to the competition – and yet he gutted it out alongside his partner.

Second, the competition setup was a little different than they had expected. For example, they had practiced with two piston ring compressors, allowing the pair to work in tandem, but the competition only permitted each team to have one.

Finally, when they arrived at the student competition, both young men were hit with nerves about the task at hand. Eirich described feeling “nauseous,” and the team was expressly worried about competing against an older team from Ferris State University.

The Arapahoe team battled through these challenges anyway. They finished first in their qualifying round but second overall, behind Ferris State, as the final round began. Less than 40 minutes later, competition judge Charles Sanville, who is known in the industry as The Humble Mechanic, observed the engine turn and signaled they had won.

“I’m still stunned by how fast these kids were,” said Bernard Tansey, a co-judge, event organizer and emcee. “The team’s preparedness and communication with each other and their coach was unparalleled. It’s obvious they put a lot of practice in, but with hundreds of people cheering just 10 feet away, it adds a level of stress and pressure you don’t get in a shop.”
Tansey owns Euro Clinic, an independent repair shop in Santa Clara, CA. He has been a dedicated volunteer and the driving force behind this competition two years in a row.
Participating schools and aftermarket sponsors

Nine teams from seven schools participated in this year’s event, which is about double the schools and triple the teams that participated in the inaugural student competition last year. It takes commitment to prepare for a competition, and courage to step on a national stage and compete, so these students have distinguished themselves from their peers.
Participating schools in the 2026 AAPEX Student Competition were:
- Advanced Training Institute, Las Vegas, NV
- Arapahoe Community College, Littleton, CO
- College of Southern Nevada, Las Vegas, NV
- Ferris State University, Grand Rapids, MI.
- North Kansas City High Schools, North Kansas City, MO
The entire event is made possible through the generosity of volunteers from the Auto Care Association Tool & Equipment Community and aftermarket businesses including:

articles.title: The Basics of Wheel Speed Sensors
articles.author: Scott Shriber

paras.en: ABS wheel speed sensors provide critical data for anti-lock braking and traction control systems. Passive sensors generate a signal using a toothed ring, while active sensors provide greater accuracy, especially at low speeds.
Technicians can diagnose sensor problems with a scan tool or digital multimeter. Counter pros should remember that ABS and traction control rely on the same wheel speed data.
This video is sponsored by the Pronto Network.

articles.title: Autel Integrates Alldata Repair With MaxiSYS Tablets
articles.author: Alex Crissey

paras.en: Autel U.S. and Alldata have partnered to connect Autel’s MaxiSYS diagnostic software with Alldata Repair on select MaxiSYS tablets. Alldata provides original equipment manufacturer (OEM) repair information. The integration connects vehicle fault codes with corresponding OEM diagnostic information, bringing scan results and repair procedures together on one screen, the companies said.
Supported models include the MaxiSYS Ultra S2, MS919 S2 and MS909 S2. The integration also supports the MaxiSYS Ultra, MS919, MS909, Ultra ADAS and Ultra EV.

From a fault code in MaxiSYS, users can open the associated Alldata information for the selected vehicle. They can review OEM code descriptions, detection criteria, possible causes and diagnostic procedures.
A split-screen view displays MaxiSYS diagnostic results alongside Alldata. This allows technicians to consult factory instructions while viewing the fault they are investigating.
Technicians can follow links within Alldata to related testing, removal and installation procedures, illustrations and service precautions.
The integration carries vehicle and fault-code information into the repair-information workflow, reducing the need for separate searches. It also helps technicians move from diagnosis to repair.

The integration also provides access to Alldata Diagnostic Intelligence, Alldata’s newest solution. It combines OEM repair information, real-world repair intelligence and AI-assisted insights in one diagnostic workflow, according to the company.

articles.title: Advics Offers More Aftermarket Brake Pads, Rotors
articles.author: Alex Crissey

paras.en: Advics announced the availability of 56 new brake pad kit SKUs and three new disc brake rotor SKUs.

The 56 new ultra-premium brake pad kit SKUs provide approximately 62.8 million vehicles in operation (VIO) axle coverage in the U.S. and Canada. The expansion covers import models including Acura, Honda, Infiniti, Mazda, Mitsubishi, Nissan, Hyundai and Kia applications.
Advics is also expanding its ultra-premium disc brake rotor line with three new SKUs for Toyota and Lexus applications, providing approximately 858,000 VIO axle coverage in the U.S. and Canada.
All three rotor SKUs are manufactured in the U.S.

articles.title: PennGrade Offers Gear Oil Fill Pouches
articles.author: Alex Crissey

paras.en: PennGrade 1 | Brad Penn has introduced new 1-quart Precision Fill Pouches for its line of gear oils.

According to the company, the pouch is designed to help reach tight and awkward fill locations where bottles can be difficult to maneuver. It features a precision-fill spout for greater control during gear oil changes and top-offs, the company added.

The new pouch format is available for PennGrade 1 | Brad Penn Multi-Purpose “Classic” Gear Oil GL-4 SAE 80W-90, designed for many traditional manual transmissions and transaxles. The formulation is specifically suited for transmissions containing brass, bronze, copper and other soft-metal components, the company added.

PennGrade 1 | Brad Penn Full Synthetic Limited Slip Gear Oils in SAE 75W-90 and SAE 75W-140 are also offered in the new pouches. These GL-5 formulations are designed for clutch-type limited slip differentials and demanding gear applications. The 75W-140 grade is specifically recommended for applications involving higher payloads and shock loading, the company notes.

articles.title: Bosch Blue Disc Brake Rotors Line Announced
articles.author: Alex Crissey

paras.en: Bosch Mobility Aftermarket announced the launch of its Bosch Blue disc brake rotors line.

According to Bosch, the rotors feature the same composition, weight and vane design as OE parts. The company touts precise machining and high-quality casting to ensure reliable braking and a long lifespan, protective paint coatings on the hat and edge, and a non-directional finish for stopping performance.

“Bosch Blue rotors were designed to give shop owners an everyday option that delivers quality, performance and value – helping end-customers get the most from their repair investment without sacrificing confident performance,” said Bobby Mathius, senior product marketing manager at Bosch Mobility Aftermarket. “With 830 total part numbers across the Bosch Blue disc brake rotors line, shop owners and technicians can confidently recommend and install Blue rotors for 95% of foreign and domestic vehicles currently on the road.”

articles.title: Autel Integrates Alldata Repair With MaxiSYS Tablets
articles.author: Alex Crissey

paras.en: Autel U.S. and Alldata have partnered to connect Autel’s MaxiSYS diagnostic software with Alldata Repair on select MaxiSYS tablets. Alldata provides original equipment manufacturer (OEM) repair information. The integration connects vehicle fault codes with corresponding OEM diagnostic information, bringing scan results and repair procedures together on one screen, the companies said.
Supported models include the MaxiSYS Ultra S2, MS919 S2 and MS909 S2. The integration also supports the MaxiSYS Ultra, MS919, MS909, Ultra ADAS and Ultra EV.

From a fault code in MaxiSYS, users can open the associated Alldata information for the selected vehicle. They can review OEM code descriptions, detection criteria, possible causes and diagnostic procedures.
A split-screen view displays MaxiSYS diagnostic results alongside Alldata. This allows technicians to consult factory instructions while viewing the fault they are investigating.
Technicians can follow links within Alldata to related testing, removal and installation procedures, illustrations and service precautions.
The integration carries vehicle and fault-code information into the repair-information workflow, reducing the need for separate searches. It also helps technicians move from diagnosis to repair.

The integration also provides access to Alldata Diagnostic Intelligence, Alldata’s newest solution. It combines OEM repair information, real-world repair intelligence and AI-assisted insights in one diagnostic workflow, according to the company.

articles.title: Momentum USA Adds 12 Brake Part Numbers
articles.author: Alex Crissey

paras.en: Momentum USA added 12 new part numbers to its brake friction and rotor catalog. This update expands coverage to over 5.3 million Vehicles in Operation (VIO) across North America.
The new products include rear brake pads for Ford commercial vans; front ceramic pads for electric vehicles; and rotors for luxury and performance vehicles.
- Ford Police Interceptor Utility & Explorer (2020–2026): Expanded coverage with the AmeriBrakes – Max Duty rear pad set (RAM2231), engineered specifically for high-stress stopping requirements.

- Hyundai, Kia & Honda: Expanded coverage across models including the Hyundai Palisade, Santa Fe, and Santa Cruz; Kia Sorento and Carnival (PTC2381); as well as the Honda HR-V and Honda Clarity (PRC2116 / CE2116).
- Cadillac Lyriq & Chevy Blazer EV (2024–2027): Targeted front ceramic pad options (PRC2521) for modern GM EV platforms.

- Mercedes-Benz, Land Rover & Volvo: Added seven new Coated and R90 Euro Rotor SKUs to serve luxury sedans, sports coupes, and performance SUVs—including Mercedes-Benz S-Class, SLK, and C-Class models, Land Rover Defender and Range Rover Sport models (537200), and the Volvo XC60 (521480).

articles.title: FTR Trucking Conditions Index Eases in September
articles.author: Kevin Linger

paras.en: FTR’s report on September 2026 trucking conditions showed its index fell to 8.13 from 11.5 in August. The company attributed the decline to record fuel costs and a pause in freight rate gains.

FTR’s revised outlook projected more favorable conditions for carriers over at least the next three quarters than it had previously forecast. The firm raised its freight volume forecast, while slow trucking employment growth pointed to constraints on adding drivers.

“Multiple signs point to a truck freight market that probably will be considerably stronger over the next few quarters than we had previously forecast,” said Avery Vise, FTR’s vice president of trucking. “Slow employment growth in trucking despite strong freight rates suggests headwinds for adding drivers, including various enforcement initiatives. An increase in our freight volume forecast puts further upward pressure on capacity utilization.”

articles.title: WIN Announces Nominations Open for ‘Founding Mothers’ Award
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: Nominations will open Nov. 16, 2026, for the Second Annual 2027 Founding Mothers Award, as announced by the Women’s Industry Network (WIN). This honor was established earlier this year to celebrate the six ‘founding mothers’ of WIN, and celebrate to organization’s creation and true mission within the collision repair industry.

Created and presented by WIN’s Founding Mothers — Frederica Carter, Geri Kottschade, Gigi Walker, Patricia Serratore, Kathy Mello, and Marcy Tieger— the award celebrates women making their mark in their shops and communities while advancing the WIN mission of supporting and connecting women in collision repair.

The Founding Mothers Award honors women who are active as technicians or painters on the shop floor, and demonstrate passion, perseverance, and purpose. Haylie Colby, a painter with Nuss Collision Center in East Bethel, Minn., became the first recipient of WIN’s inaugural Founding Mothers Award, and was presented the honor at WIN’s annual conference in May, 2026. Colby is an emerging talent in the collision repair industry and has quickly established herself as a top painter at Nuss Collision Center in just three+ years, according to WIN. What began as a part-time opportunity evolved into a full-time career, where she demonstrated skill, attention to detail, and a strong commitment to quality.

paras.en: WIN was founded 21 years ago by these six pioneering women who saw a need for connection, mentorship, and opportunity in the automotive collision industry. Their vision built the foundation for WIN’s mission to empower women across all levels of the trade. For this award, Founding Mothers Kottschade, Carter, and Tieger have actively provided input — continuing their legacy of leadership and inspiration.

“When WIN was created, they had a goal in mind of creating a safe space where shop females were welcomed, giving shops a voice and to show shops can be leaders in the collision repair industry’s organizations,” says Laura Kottschade, WIN Chair. “Key considerations for this still new, prestigious award include excellence in their craft, as well as mentoring others to success in repair excellence. The Founding Mothers Award is open to all women and annually recognizes an individual that is ‘intently involved with the true craft of collision repair, as their skills need to be still active on the shop floor – either as a hands-on refinish technician and/or painter.’”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “The annual Founding Mothers award is another continuous way for WIN to bring awareness to the availability and skills that women can successfully bring in professional collision repairs and refinishing excellence,” adds Kottschade.
Founding Mother’s Award Evaluation Criteria:
- Industry Visibility & Leadership – Inspiring others and advancing the trade
- Professional Accomplishments – Demonstrated excellence and at least two years of full‑time shop experience
- Mentorship & Support – Guiding and empowering coworkers
- Community Involvement – Promoting diversity, inclusion, and outreach

Nominations are available now through January 18, 2027 at this nominations link. This award is open to all women in the collision repair industry. Neither the nominator nor nominee is required to be a WIN member, and all nominations help WIN celebrate women who lead, mentor, and inspire a stronger, more inclusive industry. The annual winner will be announced March 22nd, and the recipient honored at WIN’s 2027 annual conference May 3-4, 2027, in Portland, Ore.
- Professional tools and equipment. Up to $3,000 toward tools or equipment of their choice

- Full conference experience. The recipient will receive an all-expenses-covered experience at the upcoming WIN Annual Conference in May, including her conference pass, lodging and round-trip flights (up to $600)
- Apparel and conference attire. $400 apparel stipend toward her conference gala attire (with any remaining to purchase workwear – jeans, polos, shoes)

articles.title: AI & the Aftermarket: AUMOVIO’s Stefan Feder
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: AftermarketNews asked executives from leading manufacturers/suppliers about how their companies are using artificial intelligence, what problems they hope to solve and how they see AI impacting their business in the coming years. It is our pleasure to share their insights and, today, we hear from Stefan Feder, Head of Automotive Aftermarket, North America, AUMOVIO Systems, Inc.
How is your company currently using artificial intelligence?

At AUMOVIO, we are applying AI across the value chain, from engineering and product development to manufacturing, knowledge management, and overall business processes. Our objective is not simply to automate existing work. It is to improve how quickly knowledge moves through the organization, how confidently decisions are made, and how effectively expertise can be scaled. This value-creating approach is true for AUMOVIO at large as well as for our aftermarket business. And to name just one example, we are currently exploring AI-supported technical assistance that could help technicians access trusted product and service information more quickly, and at the same time ensure that we do not lose the human touch that we consider very critical for the aftermarket industry. The governing principle is important: AI provides speed and scale, while people provide judgment, accountability, and context. The real opportunity comes from combining both.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Do you believe AI will change the competitive landscape of the aftermarket?

At first, the aftermarket is and will remain a people driven industry, and AI will not change that. Nevertheless, AI will have an impact on our industry as it will on many other industries. AI will change how the aftermarket makes decisions, and it can improve key performances, but it will not replace the fundamentals. It will make product quality, trusted data, technical expertise, and customer confidence even more important. The winners won’t be the companies with the most AI tools. They’ll be the ones that turn expertise and data into better decisions and performance. And ultimately become brands that both customers and AI systems confidently recommend.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Looking ahead three to five years, where do you see AI having the greatest impact on the aftermarket?

Besides further efficiency gains and helping technicians keep increasingly complex vehicles safely on the road, the greatest impact will be at the point of decision. In the short-term, AI has already started to support identifying the right part with less searching and uncertainty. Over time, the decision maker may not always be a person. A connected vehicle could recognize a service need, communicate with a repair facility and parts will be selected and procured autonomously. In that environment, the aftermarket must prepare for both human and machine customers. Our industry and the future will remain exciting, that’s for sure.

articles.title: Euclid space telescope unveils first major data release, including map of 900 million galaxies
articles.author: Brandon Specktor

paras.en: A telescope tasked with creating the largest-ever 3D map of the universe is making good on its promise.

On Thursday (Nov. 12), the European Space Agency (ESA) shared the first major data release from its Euclid space telescope, including observations of more than 900 million galaxies and 60 million black-hole-powered light sources in the early universe.

"These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos," Carole Mundell, ESA's director of science, said in a statement. "This major Euclid data release represents the largest space-based survey of its kind, laying the foundation of future discovery."

Captured over 13 months, this cornucopia of data covers a slice of sky about 9,500 bigger than the full moon — about 14% of the total sky area that Euclid will survey on its planned six-year mission. Each object in the survey is like a "puzzle piece," with its specific light signature, or spectrum), offering clues about its composition and distance from Earth, according to ESA.

Scientists can now start using the 1.7 million gigabytes of Euclid data to slot those objects into a 3D model of the universe and begin to map out the vast cosmic web that underlies all galaxies. But the data release also includes some stunning space images, which you can enjoy immediately. Here are some of the highlights.

Gravitational lenses are nature's biggest magnifying glasses. These "Einstein rings" — named after Albert Einstein, who predicted their existence — occur when exceptionally massive objects, like large galaxies, bend the fabric of space-time. This cosmic curvature causes the light emitted by objects behind them to appear magnified, distorted and sometimes duplicated.

In its first data release, Euclid has discovered more than 15,000 strong gravitational lensing candidates. These cosmic lenses enable astronomers to get much clearer views of the deep universe than any telescope could possibly see on its own.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Over 10 years ago, we forecast that Euclid would revolutionise the field of strong lens discovery," Natalie Lines, a Euclid Consortium member working at the University of Portsmouth in the UK, said in the statement. "That day is finally here."
The Messier 81 galaxy (seen on the right) is one of the brightest in the sky. With fully developed spiral arms stretching to its bright core, M81 is known as a "grand design spiral" galaxy.

While M81 is relatively close to Earth and can be seen with a good pair of binoculars, Euclid's field of view captures it alongside the elliptical galaxy NGC 3077 (bottom left) and crisp clouds of interstellar dust.

Among the nearly 1 billion galaxies charted by Euclid is NGC 1291, also called the Golden Eye galaxy. The galaxy is located 33 million light-years from Earth, and Euclid shows a close-up view of it here at the telescope's highest resolution, according to ESA.
Ring galaxies like this contain a central bulge disconnected from a surrounding ring of stars; astronomers think these galaxies form when a smaller galaxy plunges through the middle of a larger one.

This image shows the entire sector of the Euclid Wide Survey, the telescope's mission to map vast swatches of the northern sky. The Wide Survey is accompanied by the Euclid Deep Survey, which will spend about 10% of the telescope's observing time taking repeated observations of three relatively small spots of sky, according to ESA.

With about 85% of its survey left to go, Euclid is on track to collect one of the most comprehensive datasets of the universe ever. Now, it'll be up to the scientific community to make good use of those observations and find something extraordinary.
For more stunning space images, check out our Space Photo of the Week.

Brandon is the space / physics editor at Live Science. With more than 20 years of editorial experience, his writing has appeared in The Washington Post, Reader's Digest, CBS.com, the Richard Dawkins Foundation website and other outlets. He holds a bachelor's degree in creative writing from the University of Arizona, with minors in journalism and media arts. His interests include black holes, asteroids and comets, and the search for extraterrestrial life.

articles.title: When a battery dies, you replace it — how jumpstarting cells with fresh mitochondria could revolutionize medicine
articles.author: Nicoletta Lanese

paras.en: A newborn baby's heart is roughly the size of a walnut — which makes open-heart surgery challenging.

Each year, about 10,000 babies in the United States are born with critical heart defects that may require surgery to fix, often fairly soon after birth. In these infants, the two major arteries of the heart could have swapped positions or the left side of the heart may be far too small to pump properly.

Even if their surgeries go well, these babies face perilous recoveries. A complication can arise when blood flows back into the repaired heart, triggering what's known as an ischemia-reperfusion injury. This can stun the organ, triggering extensive damage that requires doctors to place the baby on a life-support machine that pumps and infuses oxygen into blood to sub in for the hampered heart and lungs. Only about 40% of newborns make it off the machine, because often, their tiny hearts don't recover.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Doctors and scientists at Boston Children's Hospital have been working to improve those odds using a creative idea: replacing the fuel source in damaged heart cells to help them bounce back from injury. That fuel source is mitochondria, the "batteries" found in most cells in the body. In this case, the mitochondria are isolated from an abdominal muscle and then injected directly into the heart.

As of April, 17 babies have undergone this procedure, and 80% made it off ECMO. It's too soon to say if the treatment improves overall survival rates, but the early data hints that it might. A clinical trial is currently underway.

"The first one or two for me were pretty nerve-wracking," said James McCully, a research associate at Boston Children's Hospital and associate professor of surgery at Harvard Medical School whose pioneering work paved the way for these procedures. His team isolates and purifies the mitochondria that a surgical team then transplants into patients.

"But you know, the heart comes back — you can actually almost see it coming back" in real time, he told Live Science. A heart deprived of energy looks pallid, while a freshly rejuvenated heart blushes a healthy pink.

Baby heart infusions are just one example of the promise of "mitochondrial transplantation." Following McCully's lead, other scientists have started investigating whether infusions of mitochondria could revitalize donated organs destined for transplantation, help stroke patients recover, and treat kids with devastating diseases. This work is still highly experimental, and its route to regulatory approval remains unclear.
But at its core is a straightforward idea: When a battery dies, you replace it.

The human body contains tens of trillions of cells, most of which contain hundreds to thousands of mitochondria. Following some back-of-the-envelope math, that means the total potential energy in each person "is the equivalent of a lightning bolt," Douglas Wallace, director of the Center for Mitochondrial and Epigenomic Medicine at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, told attendees last year at a symposium on mitochondrial medicine.

Mitochondria, in a word, are powerful. They produce most of the chemical energy used by complex cells by churning out a molecule called adenosine triphosphate (ATP). The idea of transferring these fuel factories from one cell to another as a medical treatment emerged less than two decades ago — but cells have been doing such swaps on their own for eons.

Dr. Jon Brestoff, an associate professor of pathology and immunology and director of the Immunometabolism Initiative at the Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, describes this ability to move from cell to cell as a relic of mitochondria's bacterial past. "It is hypothesized that mitochondria transfer has likely been retained throughout evolution of eukaryotic life," the huge domain of life that includes all plants, fungi, protists and animals, Brestoff told Live Science.

Mitochondria are the powerhouses of nearly all complex cells on Earth, and there are a few theories as to how they adopted that ubiquitous role. A leading idea posits that, some 1.5 billion to 2 billion years ago, one simple cell engulfed another. The bacterial cell that got swallowed carried a circular loop of DNA inside its membrane, and that captured cell later became what we now know as the mitochondrion. The new organelle enabled cells to take advantage of the abundance of oxygen on our planet by converting it into usable fuel.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Mitochondria retained bacteria-like features, such as having their own DNA and membranes. But in 2006, researchers reported that mitochondria can also exit their "host" and survive the journey into a totally different cell — a phenomenon known as mitochondrial transfer.

"That was a complete revolution in thinking," said Dr. Lance Becker, professor and Chair of the Department of Emergency Medicine at Northwell Health and the Feinstein Institutes for Medical Research. "With that notion that mitochondria might be mobile, that they might cross boundaries, that they might go from one cell to another cell, came the possibility that maybe that was something we could use to help people."

The 2006 study showed that cells that had been depleted of their own mitochondrial DNA could obtain healthy mitochondria from neighboring cells. After receiving other cells' powerhouses, the once-depleted cells were able to conduct energetically costly processes, such as cell division.

This research provided the first evidence that one cell can "donate" metabolic properties to its neighbor by sending over a fresh batch of mitochondria. Scientists once thought cells had to make all of their own mitochondria, but now, "I think cells have the ability to 'put their hand up' when they need mitochondria," Becker told Live Science.

Because those first experiments were done in lab dishes, initially, "it was unclear whether or not it was really biologically meaningful or relevant," Brestoff said. But within the past five to six years, improved tools and techniques have enabled scientists to watch mitochondrial transfer unfold within living organisms, he noted. It's been shown that cells of the same type can exchange mitochondria, as can cells of different types.
As scientists' fundamental understanding of mitochondrial transfer grew, the notion of doing the same thing therapeutically gained more traction.
"That procedure," Brestoff said, "is rooted in the biology of mitochondria transfer."
Just two years after the landmark 2006 paper, McCully's research group released data that hinted at the medicinal potential of mitochondrial transplantation.

Since then, these complementary lines of research — the foundational biology and the preclinical investigation — have continued in parallel. McCully's preclinical work helped to inspire other labs to explore the use of mitochondrial transplantation for a range of medical applications, including organ transplants and treatments for stroke and genetic disease.

McCully is "the pioneer — the guru of the field," said Dr. Giuseppe Orlando, a professor of surgery and regenerative medicine at Wake Forest University School of Medicine who is exploring mitochondrial transplantation as a way to maintain the integrity of transplant organs.

McCully's road to mitochondrial transplantation started in the 1980s. As a molecular biologist, he wanted to uncover mechanisms that protect the heart from damage, particularly when the organ's oxygen supply is compromised — such as during ischemia, or low blood flow. With an eye on older adults, he wanted to spare patients' heart tissue from the damage and cell death that can occur before and during heart surgery.

McCully and his collaborators initially "didn't care about the mitochondria one iota," he said. They were more focused on the nucleus, the control center that houses most of a cell's DNA, and its influence on cellular pathways that might boost the heart's resilience to ischemia. But "what we found was that everything we did started coming back to the mitochondria," he said.

They found that ischemia triggers damage and dysfunction in mitochondria that persists even after the heart's oxygen supply is restored; this dysfunction ultimately kills cells. The damaged mitochondria swell up, leak their innards, and set off a chain reaction that causes a cell to self-destruct.

McCully and colleagues observed that biological pathways that seemed to reduce this cell death often centered on the mitochondria. "We were looking around at either pathways upstream of the mitochondria or downstream of the mitochondria," he said.

So, logically, they started looking directly at mitochondria, studying what the organelle looks like before, during and after ischemia. One day, while isolating mitochondria from a laboratory pig, the animal developed fibrillation, meaning its heart began beating very quickly, with an uncoordinated and rapid rhythm. The team tried to reset the heart's rhythm with electric shocks and medications, to no avail. But McCully had an idea.

"At that point in time, the heart's kind of [got a] gray pallor, and it looks dead," he said. "And I said, 'Go upstairs; grab some of those mitochondria that we've isolated from the non-ischemic type. Just bring them down.'" They'd previously gathered some healthy mitochondria from the same pig, in hopes of generating a "before-and-after" picture of ischemia. Instead, McCully suspended those healthy mitochondria in a solution and then injected them directly into the pig's fibrillating heart.
"And the heart came back — started beating normally. It changed color, went back to a pink hue, and just kept on going," he said.
Surgeons sample a small piece of muscle from the patient. That muscle will serve as the source of healthy mitochondria.
After mitochondria have been isolated from the muscle sample, they are prepared in a syringe and injected into the heart tissue.

That serendipitous experiment led to a formal test of the technique in rabbit hearts, the results of which were published in 2008. In the study, they introduced healthy mitochondria to the rabbits' hearts during ischemia, just before reperfusion — when blood is reintroduced into the oxygen-starved tissue. They found that the mitochondria improved the organs' recovery and reduced tissue death. Further research in animals suggested that mitochondria that originated from one type of tissue, like liver tissue or skeletal muscle, could be introduced to other tissue types, such as cardiac muscle.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: After seeing McCully's results in various animal experiments, including more with pigs, Dr. Pedro del Nido, chair of cardiac surgery at Boston Children's and a professor of child surgery at Harvard Medical School, approached him about testing the technique in human patients — namely, in babies on a life-support machine known as ECMO.
"He saw it in the animals; he saw what was going on," McCully said. "And he deemed it as being a possible intervention to save these kids."

They sought permission from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to test the procedure and cleared the required regulatory hurdles. The process was made slightly easier because the mitochondria were coming from the patients' own bodies, not from a donor, McCully noted. Once given the go-ahead, they set forth with the help of Dr. Sitaram Emani, a heart surgeon at Boston Children's. The first procedure took place in 2014.

During each procedure, Emani and the surgical team collect a small sample of skeletal muscle from the patient, and McCully then isolates whole mitochondria from the tissue and prepares them in a syringe. He refined the isolation technique so the time from collecting the muscle sample to injecting mitochondria is only 30 minutes. Lately, the team has been developing a technique they can perform in the operating room, rather than in a lab, which could cut the time to 20 minutes. Emani uses various tests, including echocardiography, to see which areas of the heart tissue move the least, and injects mitochondria straight into those areas.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: "It's great to be able to see something you've done and worked on for so many years actually provide a benefit," McCully said.
While McCully is trying to protect infant hearts, other scientists want to do the same for other organs — including those destined for transplant surgeries.

To Orlando, mitochondria represent a potential way to make donated kidneys work better. "In transplant medicine, one of the major issues is making sure that the organs that are procured are well stored and kept viable until implantation," said Orlando, who is also president of the Cell Transplant and Regenerative Medicine Society.

Maintaining an organ's viability means preserving mitochondrial function as much as possible, but the transplantation process is tough on the organelles. "That energy plant is damaged. So it's pretty obvious that you should start thinking about a way to replace the damaged mitochondria," Orlando said.

Donated organs suffer some damage when they're unplugged from the donors' bloodstream, in part because this cuts off mitochondria's crucial oxygen supply. And then, paradoxically, the donor organs also get damaged when they're plugged into the recipient's bloodstream. That's because the fast flow of blood triggers the production of free radicals — unstable molecules that damage tissues.

While healthy organs normally produce some free radicals, reperfusion unleashes a flood. "It's more than the organ can bear and sustain," Orlando explained. This damage contributes to a phenomenon called delayed graft function, in which a transplanted kidney doesn't work right away so the patient ends up needing dialysis in the first week after surgery.
"You want to make sure that the kidney wakes up faster," Orlando said. That's where mitochondria come in.

Orlando was introduced to the idea of mitochondrial transplantation around 2019 through a collaboration with Dr. Benedetta Bussolati, a nephrologist and full professor of laboratory medicine at the University of Turin in Italy. Her lab had been studying mitochondrial transplantation in isolated kidney cells in lab experiments, and they reached out to Orlando about extending that work to lab animals.

In pigs, the researchers ran experiments in which the animals' kidneys were collected and stored in the same way human kidneys commonly would be prior to being transplanted. One set of kidneys received a placebo treatment, while another got an infusion of mitochondria from the donor pigs' muscle tissue. Upon being reperfused, the treated kidneys produced fewer free radicals and accrued less damage than the untreated kidneys did, the team reported in 2023.

They backed up this finding by analyzing RNA, a molecule that reflects which genes are active in cells. Compared with the untreated kidneys, the treated kidneys showed greater activity in genes involved in mitochondrial metabolism and lower activity in genes involved in repairing injuries.

Some groups are exploring mitochondrial transplantation in other donor organs, like the lungs — specifically, lungs treated with "ex vivo perfusion" (EVP), an emerging approach that helps retain the viability of transplant organs. Rather than placing a donor organ in a cooler of ice, as is generally standard, EVP flushes an organ with nutrient- and oxygen-rich fluid, helping to maintain its function until the transplant surgery. In lab experiments with pig and human lungs, scientists found that introducing fresh mitochondria during EVP further improved the organs' function while reducing inflammation and free radicals.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Across different organ transplants, Orlando sees mitochondria as a potential means to improve patient outcomes and expand the pool of available organs. There are scenarios in which would-be organ donors die unexpectedly of cardiac arrest and their organs are damaged in the process; mitochondrial transplants may help make such organs fit for patients, Orlando has said.

In the near term, Orlando and his colleagues are continuing to study the basic science of mitochondrial transplantation for this clinical purpose; they've also been cleared to run a clinical trial with donor kidneys but need more funds to proceed.

Looking to the more distant future, he and other experts in the field envision a world where transplant organs can be bioengineered and stored in banks, ready and waiting for the patients who need them, Orlando said. If that vision materializes, he suggested, mitochondrial transplants might be useful for preparing banked organs for transplantation "by giving them kind of an energy boost."

If infusions of fresh mitochondria could help the heart, kidney and lungs, what about the brain? That's the question Dr. Melanie Walker and colleagues at the University of Washington School of Medicine (UW Medicine) want to answer.

Walker, a clinical professor of neurological surgery, treats patients who have had ischemic strokes, which are caused by blood clots blocking blood flow to the brain. The immediate aim of post-stroke treatment is to clear out the blocked "pipe" and restore circulation to the brain as quickly as possible, she said. But no matter how quickly this is done, some brain cells are damaged. And once the blood clot is removed, the brain may then suffer a reperfusion injury.

Standard treatments can dissolve the clot but don't protect the brain, Walker said. "What about all those cells that are maybe not quite dead — they're on the verge of maybe dying? What can we do to support those guys?" she asked.

The UW Medicine team had heard about McCully's work in Boston and wondered if something similar could be applied in stroke patients. But while heart surgery exposes the tissue in need of new mitochondria, accessing the brain is trickier. "You don't do a craniotomy to give an IV medicine," Walker told Live Science.

But Walker realized that a harmful downstream effect of stroke might provide an opportunity for treatment. Immediately after a stroke, the brain's protective shield — known as the blood-brain barrier — becomes more permeable than usual, allowing more substances to pass from the bloodstream into brain tissue. That might open a door for mitochondrial transplantation.

A 2023 mouse study spearheaded by University of Virginia researchers and co-authored by Walker backed this idea, finding that mitochondria entered the brain after stroke and integrated into brain cells. These mitochondria had been gathered from muscle tissue, as in McCully's studies, and introduced to the brain via an artery. The treatment increased ATP production while reducing cell death caused by the stroke, compared with untreated mice's brains.

This work paved the way to the first trial using mitochondrial transplant in the human brain. The small safety trial included adult patients who'd had ischemic strokes and underwent thrombectomies — surgeries to remove the clots from their blood vessels. Four received mitochondrial transplants during their procedures and 12 did not. Mitochondria were injected near the site of each patient's stroke, into the closest branch of one of the brain's major arteries.

No negative side effects were tied to the transplants, hinting that the procedure is safe in humans. "But the next question is, how do we understand if it helps? And those are harder trials to design," Walker said. That's partly because the transplants are tacked onto the clot-removal procedure, so it's difficult to separate their effects from those of the clot removal itself, she noted.

Future trials will also need to explore exactly where the transplanted mitochondria end up in the human brain, how well they function once inside brain cells, and how the dose and timing of the transplant affect patients' outcomes, the trial runners wrote in their report. For the moment, Walker said her team is focused on exploring the safety aspects of the approach and have no further trials planned at this time.
Mitochondrial diseases — and what's next

Beyond heart defects, transplant organs and stroke, researchers are looking to mitochondrial transplantation as a solution for genetic conditions that harm mitochondria directly. Brestoff and colleagues are investigating the therapy's potential for treating Leigh syndrome, a rare neurological condition caused by genetic mutations that disrupt the fuel-producing machinery in mitochondria.

"Those kids have a terrible prognosis," Brestoff said. Most children with the most common form of the syndrome, whose symptoms show up by age 2, die by age 3. There is no cure for the syndrome, and treatments to relieve its symptoms are limited. So if it works, mitochondrial transplantation could fill a big gap.

So far, the approach shows promise in lab mice with a severe form of Leigh syndrome, improving the rodents' function and extending their median lifespan by 19% to 24%, the researchers demonstrated in 2024. They're now studying the approach in cells derived from patients with the disease.

Some companies, such as Israel-headquartered Minovia Therapeutics, are already running clinical trials with patients with other types of mitochondrial disease. Minovia is running one with children with Pearson syndrome, in which missing mitochondrial DNA hinders the function of bone marrow, which normally makes blood and immune cells.

While patients with a heart or brain problem may be able to pluck mitochondria from healthy muscles, people with mitochondrial disease don't necessarily have healthy mitochondria to spare. Especially for these patients, getting mitochondria from other people — known as heterologous transplantation — likely makes the most sense. What's more, for transplantation to be used widely for any purpose, there would need to be an "off-the-shelf" mitochondrial product available, Brestoff said.

Such a product could eliminate the step in Boston Children's heart procedure where mitochondria have to be isolated from a patient while they're waiting, open on an operating table. "Getting them from the recipient can sometimes be problematic, because the recipients are sick. All the organs, all the tissue is quite distressed," McCully noted. A standardized and safety-tested mitochondrial product would therefore be a boon for the field.

Brestoff is on the scientific advisory board of LUCA Science, a company developing mitochondria as therapeutic agents, and a consultant for Cellergy Therapeutics, which is making mitochondrial products to combat conditions from muscle degeneration and aging. These companies exemplify the effort to come up with ready-made products that could someday bring the therapy to more patients.

A shift to heterologous transplantation does raise concerns about immune reactions. "You have some variations in the proteins that are present in your mitochondria that I don't have," Brestoff noted. "So it is possible that our immune systems recognize heterologous mitochondria as non-self."

But McCully doesn't expect immune reactions to be a big problem, based on his research in animals. "I can get the mitochondria from you and put them into me, me into you — doesn't really matter," he said. Early trial results from Minovia and others suggest heterologous transplantations come with minimal side effects, at least at doses tested so far.
- Neanderthal DNA still survives in our human family tree. What were our ancient relatives' relationships like?
- Adversity shaped our evolution as a species. People raised in it may have underrecognized strengths because of it.
- Psychedelics may rewire the brain to treat PTSD. Scientists are finally beginning to understand how.
Another roadblock is that the FDA has not approved any organelles as therapies yet, so the standards and regulatory framework for the field are still being established, Brestoff said.

Despite that hurdle, the field has advanced significantly since its start as a niche, theoretical interest and then a highly experimental procedure for the sickest newborns. Scientists are now exploring the treatment as a solution to many common conditions, from rheumatoid arthritis to chronic pain.
Becker compared the state of the field to the early days of organ transplantation.
"It just turned out that it was revolutionary, when all of a sudden you could just give a person a kidney transplant," he said. "I think it's going to be kind of similar with mitochondria."

articles.title: 'Like writing and directing your own movie': Live Science readers share whether they'd learn to lucid dream if they could
articles.author: Nicoletta Lanese

paras.en: Lucid dreaming describes when you realize you're in a dream as it's unfolding. Sometimes, people can control the content of their dreams from this state of awareness.

Recently, researchers claimed that they found a way to "train" people to lucid dream by having them meditate and complete virtual-reality-augmented exercises while they were awake. Following the release of that study, Live Science asked its readers whether they would learn to lucid dream if they could.

Over 300 readers weighed in, with 77% saying "Yes, I'd want to try to control my dreams." Additionally, 17% of respondents said "No, I already lucid dream enough without training," 3% said "No, I don't see the point," and the final 3% said they weren't sure.

In the comments, one reader shared that they'd once experimented with hypnagogic napping, a technique famously used by Thomas Edison and Salvador Dalí in which the famous luminaries would wake themselves up just as they were drifting to sleep. Edison claimed that this helped him access a creative sweet spot at the edge of sleep and wakefulness.

"When I was experimenting with the hypnagogic state (using the Edison method) I started having spontaneous lucid dreams," the reader wrote. "I can confidently say, that there were some of the most profound experiences of my life, so the answer is definitely yes."

Another reader reported having lucid dreams "about once or twice a year," adding that they typically wake up shortly after realizing it's a dream. "My most recent one was of my recently deceased wife. I became very sad when I realized she wasn't supposed to be there," the reader wrote. "I hugged her and told her I don't want to be without her. She replied that I could live a long life if I took care of myself (This was a very typical response from her...lol). I feel very blessed to have had that dream."
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Other readers chimed in on Facebook. "Already have it [lucid dreaming], but if I didn't I would certainly practice to do so," one wrote. "Hell yes," another said, in response to the idea of training themselves to lucid dream.

Other readers noted that they already lucid dream quite often or that they can consistently control their dreams, with one even saying that all of their dreams are lucid. Another said, "Some nights I interrupt it [my dream] like Monty Python — 'Too silly!' and start over."

But while one person compared lucid dreaming to "writing and directing your own movie," another noted that "lucid dreams can be boring, repetitive, annoying." So while many people would practice lucid dreaming if they could, not everyone sees the appeal.
