paras.en: Las Vegas GP 2026: Dates, schedule, weather, UK start time and how to watch or stream F1 race in United States live on Sky Sports

Find out the race-week schedule, weather and how to watch the Las Vegas Grand Prix at The Strip Circuit; watch every session live on Sky Sports F1, with qualifying at 4am on Saturday November 21 and the race at 4am on Sunday November 22
Formula 1 heads for the bright lights of Las Vegas with both 2026 titles settled, but the competitive picture at the front of the grid tighter than it has been at any other stage of the season.

The Las Vegas Strip Circuit opens the triple header of events that conclude the campaign with the race on the streets of Sin City quickly followed by a fortnight in the Middle East for the Qatar and Abu Dhabi Grands Prix.

Last time out at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, Mercedes completed a title double by sealing the Constructors' Championship a week on from Kimi Antonelli becoming F1's youngest ever world champion at the Mexico City Grand Prix.
- F1 2026 Calendar | F1 2026 Standings | F1 Gossip Column
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream F1 with no contract 📺
Despite closing out both championships, Mercedes are actually enduring their most difficult period of the season, with their rivals regularly outperforming them.

McLaren's Lando Norris claimed his third win of the season in Brazil, while Ferrari may well have claimed a one-two the weekend before in Mexico had Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc not clashed on the first lap.

Max Verstappen has featured on the last eight podiums, a run which has moved the Red Bull driver 17 points clear of Antonelli's team-mate George Russell in the battle for second in the standings, with Hamilton just a point further back.
The race for third in the constructors' standings is also very much on, with Red Bull just 17 points clear of McLaren. The duel for seventh is also tight with Haas only three points ahead of Audi.
That will ensure there is plenty to play for as F1 makes its fourth appearance at the stunning street circuit since Las Vegas returned to the sport's calendar in 2023.
With all track sessions running in the late afternoon or evening local time in Vegas, which is eight hours behind the UK and Ireland.

Sky Sports F1 viewers need to set their alarms - or, in the case of first and final practice, perhaps just stay up late - to watch the weekend's sessions live. Qualifying and the Grand Prix itself both start at 4am GMT.
Full F1 session re-runs will also be shown on Sky Sports F1 and Main Event each morning, while there will also be highlights available to watch on the Sky Sports website and app.
Las Vegas GP track - Las Vegas Strip Circuit
Considered F1's most ambitious project to bring racing to the heart of Las Vegas and the city's world-renowned Strip, the street track runs to 3.8 miles in length and features 17 corners.
The layout winds past some of Vegas' most famous landmarks, such as the Venetian, the Bellagio Fountains and the Eiffel Tower at Paris, and features a 1.2-mile flat-out blast down the Strip.

With an average speed of 150mph across Russell's dry-weather pole position lap in 2024 (2025's qualifying was wet), Vegas represents F1's second-fastest street track after the Jeddah Corniche Circuit in Saudi Arabia. It has also proved itself to be good for racing, with plenty of overtaking and action over the first three years.
With the race again taking place late in November, the 2026 edition is set to follow the pattern of the first three events in terms of weather conditions.

Day-time temperatures in the mid-high teens are set to be followed by chilly evenings as temperatures drop towards single figures in Nevada's Mojave Desert. No rain is currently forecast during track days.

articles.title: Senior U.S. Army soldier arrested in U.K. on suspicion of assisting Russian intelligence
articles.author: Courtney Kube

paras.en: LONDON — A senior U.S. Army soldier was arrested in the U.K. on suspicion of assisting Russian intelligence, British police said Tuesday.

The 41-year-old man was arrested “as part of an investigation by Counter Terrorism Policing” near the city of Gloucester, in the west of England, London’s Metropolitan Police said in a statement, adding that he remained in custody at a police station in London.

He was arrested on suspicion of offenses under sections 1 and 3 of the National Security Act, the statement said. They relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service.
“The country to which the allegations relate is Russia,” the statement added.

Three people familiar with the matter told NBC News that the soldier was based at NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps headquarters at Imjin Barracks on the outskirts of Gloucester. A senior NATO military official also confirmed the location of the soldier’s assignment.

FBI Director Kash Patel was quoted in the statement as saying that the arrest was “important” and that it “involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies.”
The FBI, he added, “has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners.”

Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, was quoted in the police statement as saying, “The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent.”said.

“This case demonstrates the strength of our partnerships and the resolve of the counterintelligence community,” he added. “I am grateful to the U.K. and the FBI for their professionalism and teamwork throughout this investigation.”
Calling the allegations “very serious,” Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, Britain’s senior national coordinator for counterterrorism policing, said the “investigation is very much ongoing.”
The investigation is not linked to any other ongoing counterterrorism operations, the statement said.
The arrest comes at a time of heightened tensions around the threat from hostile states, with British security services saying Russia and Iran have both used proxies to commit crimes on U.K. soil.

Officials in the U.K. have said proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arson fires and other attacks in Britain and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear.
The U.S. has moved military aircraft from an air base in the U.K. amid threats from Iran.
A U.S. official confirmed to NBC News that several military aircraft had left RAF Mildenhall as the security posture there had increased.
At least eight air refueling tankers and three Osprey tilt-rotor military transports left the base in Suffolk, eastern England, on Monday, flight tracking data showed.

articles.title: U.S. charges 3 men with plotting multiple terror attacks, including on British air base
articles.author: Michael Kosnar

paras.en: Three men, including one already jailed in the U.S., were accused by U.S. authorities Tuesday of being Iran-supported operatives who plotted nearly 20 attacks on Jewish communities in Europe and the U.S., as well as a planned assault on a British air base used by the U.S. Air Force.

Charges against Mohammad Al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali Al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, were outlined in a superseding indictment unsealed in federal court in New York City.
Only Al-Saadi — an alleged pro-Iranian terrorist who is believed to have plotted attacks across Europe, Canada and the U.S., as first reported by NBC News — is in custody.

U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald in New York said in a news release that Al-Saadi, who was arrested in the spring, continued to coordinate with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted September terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, where U.S. bombers and troops had been stationed.

“As alleged, these defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” said McDonald, whose office is handling the case.
“The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real,” he added in the statement.

The new indictment offers fresh insight into an episode that has been shrouded in mystery for more than a month after five men were detained after midnight Sept. 27 on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward the base in western England.

The Justice Department indictment alleges that Al-Hassani paid associates to carry out surveillance of RAF Fairford in August and paid several people to move forward with the plot in September “by procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel.”
The group even made custom decals to give the vans the appearance that they were used by a fuel company and a swimming pool supply business, authorities say.
Al-Hassani is alleged to have then tasked the people to go to the base with the fuel when U.K. law enforcement took the men into custody.

Al-Saadi was helping direct the RAF Fairford plot while he was in a U.S. prison, according to the indictment. He made video and phone calls to his family members in Iraq, who are alleged to have passed coded messages to Al-Hassani and Mohajeri.
In a July call with his sister, Al-Saadi asked, “What are we doing about all our old work?” — a reference to terrorist activity — according to investigators.
His sister replied, “It isn’t cancelled,” investigators said.
In June, Al-Saadi pleaded not guilty to charges that he plotted at least 18 attacks in Europe in retaliation for the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran.

But the indictment alleges that the three men conspired to use a network of contacts in the United Kingdom to commit terrorist attacks on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata’ib Hizballah.

The European attacks “were carried out in the name of a purportedly new terrorist group with the pseudonym Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (“HAYI”), which is actually a front for Kata’ib Hizballah,” the release said.
The U.S. government has designated Kata’ib Hizballah and the Revolutionary Guards as foreign terrorist organizations.

articles.title: Hung jury in trial of man accused of Busselton 'love triangle' murder
articles.author: David Weber

paras.en: A man accused of murdering a woman in WA's South West is set to face a retrial, after a jury could not reach a verdict.
James Anthony Sorgiovanni had been accused of stabbing Tara Morrison to death.
The jury had been deliberating since Monday.
The jury in the trial of a man accused of murdering a woman whose body was found stuffed in a wardrobe at a house in WA’s South West has been unable to reach a verdict.
WARNING: The following story contains details that may distress some readers.
James Anthony Sorgiovanni, 29, had been on trial for the murder of Tara Morrison, whose body was found in his Busselton house in 2024.
Ms Morrison had been visiting the house Mr Sorgiovanni shared with his girlfriend Hannah Louise Glover, who had also been charged with murder but pleaded guilty part-way through the trial.
Her guilty plea followed the evidence of an inmate who said Glover — who was formerly Ms Morrison's girlfriend — had confessed to the killing in prison.
The court was earlier told Ms Morrison was killed in a frenzied attack arising from a “love triangle”.
The jury started deliberating on Monday afternoon but after days of discussing the case, could not reach a unanimous verdict on the charge of murder and was discharged today.
Glover gave evidence describing how she stabbed her former girlfriend multiple times, in several locations inside the house she shared with Mr Sorgiovanni.
She told the jury Mr Sorgiovanni held Ms Morrison while Glover attacked her, but that he was the last one to stab the victim.
The court had heard Ms Morrison was planning to stay at the house, and methylamphetamine and GHB were used on the night of the murder.
Mr Sorgiovanni’s lawyer Lisa Boston told the jury he was under the influence of drugs at the time, woke to find Glover attacking Ms Morrison, and could not effectively prevent it.
Under cross-examination by Ms Boston, the prisoner who Glover confessed to said Glover made "no mention" of Mr Sorgiovanni initially.
She said Glover told her Mr Sorgiovanni had grabbed her in a "bear hug" and tried to drag her away.
During closing submissions to the jury, prosecutor Michael Cvetkoski showed a photo of Tara Morrison's left hand, with a serious injury which he described as a defensive wound.
Mr Cvetkoski put it to the jury that Ms Morrison's right hand was being restrained and could not be used as a "defensive mechanism".
"Likely, this was an ongoing struggle," Mr Cvetkoski told the jury.
The court was shown crime scene photos with blood on the floor and walls of the house.
It is not known when Glover will be sentenced.

articles.title: Man who burned shoebox of tax records fined for resulting bushfire
articles.author: Duncan Bailey

paras.en: A Tasmanian man has been convicted and fined over a fire he lit in the state's upper east coast that later destroyed two homes.
Michael John Davis was found guilty of lighting a fire without taking reasonable precautions to prevent it from spreading.
Davis was fined a total of $3,000 on two charges, one relating to drink driving.
A Tasmanian man has been fined for lighting a fire that destroyed two houses and burnt through 1,200 hectares of vegetation in the state's upper east coast.
Michael John Davis, 56, was found guilty in the Launceston Magistrates Court this week of lighting a fire on December 9 last year without taking reasonable precautions to prevent it from spreading.
He also pleaded guilty to a low-range drink-driving charge.
According to his lawyer, James Oxley, Davis could not appear in person as he lives in Indonesia, and so appeared via videolink.
The prosecution said on December 9, 2025, Mr Davis was at his parents' property burning a shoebox filled with tax records inside a fire pit while smoking cigarettes.
Davis sat with the fire until the box had burnt completely, then went inside to prepare lunch for his father, who was bedridden at the time.
When he went back outside 30 minutes later, he discovered bushland on the northern boundary of the home, metres from where he burnt the receipts, was on fire.
Davis attempted to extinguish the fire with buckets of water and asked his mother to call the fire brigade when she returned home.
The fire had spread through bushland to the north, and as a result, two residences on St Helens Point Road were destroyed.
TasNetworks and Telstra infrastructure were also damaged as a result of the fire.
Mr Oxley said he confirmed with the Tasmania Fire Service that a total fire ban had not been issued on the day, and no fire permits were required in that area.
He said the total number of documents burnt had fit into a shoebox, and that the fire was not large.
"At its most intense it was about a foot high (30 centimetres) while the documents burned,"
"He did everything he could once he saw the fire had spread to put it out."

Mr Oxley asked Magistrate Simon Brown to consider Davis' visa status in his decision, and asked for Davis to be fined without a conviction, as that could hamper his chances at renewing his visa with the Indonesian government.
"That process will involve him producing his Tasmanian record to the Indonesian government," he said.
"His plan is to remain there with his wife for the foreseeable future, and in my submission there is a real risk that this could come back to haunt him in that application process."
However, Magistrate Brown said there had been "catastrophic consequences" as a result of Davis' negligence.
"In fairness, I don't think I'm minded to not convict," he said.
"I accept the defendant's degree of negligence. His moral culpability here is plainly at the lower end of the scale.
"Of course, lighting a fire outside in Tasmania in the summer months in December is something that should be done with real care.
"Whilst the defendant did watch the fire and believed it to be out, he took no steps to ensure it could go absolutely nowhere by wetting down or stamping on it."
Magistrate Brown convicted Davis and fined him $1,000 for the drink driving charge, as well as suspended his licence for six months.
He was fined $2,000 in relation to the fire, totalling $3,000.

articles.title: Australia's next fast bowling star blows England away on ODI debut

paras.en: Mon, 14 Sept, 11:00 pm, Final score, ZIM 235, AUS 8/294
Australia's Mahli Beardman blows England away on ODI debut in Perth
Mahli Beardman took a scintillating 6–24 on his ODI debut against England in Perth.
The 21-year-old quick removed Harry Brook and Joe Root for his first two wickets.
Australia requires 132 for victory in the first game of a three-game series.

articles.title: Indonesia's vice-president resigns after academic credentials questioned

paras.en: Indonesia's vice-president resigns after academic credentials questioned
Gibran Rakabuming Raka offered to resign during a meeting with President Prabowo Subianto
Indonesia's vice-president resigned Thursday as questions grew over his eligibility for the office after recent court rulings disputed his educational credentials.

Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the 39-year-old son of former president Joko Widodo, submitted his resignation to the leadership of the People's Consultative Assembly, the country's highest legislative body, at the parliament building in the capital, Jakarta.

Raka had offered to resign Tuesday during a meeting with President Prabowo Subianto, saying he wanted to avoid a prolonged political controversy. But a Cabinet minister said the president urged Raka at the time to defend himself and it wasn't clear if he accepted the resignation offer.
The Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court ruled last month that the documents Raka submitted regarding his overseas education didn't meet election requirements.
A subsequent petition, submitted Wednesday to the House leadership by 120 lawmakers from eight political parties, began a parliamentary process that could lead to his impeachment.

Under Indonesian law, House leaders must establish a special committee to examine whether Raka has violated the constitution by serving as vice president, despite allegedly failing to meet election requirements.
If lawmakers determine there is sufficient basis for the accusation, the House must ask the Constitutional Court to rule on whether a constitutional violation has occurred.
The academic credentials investigation was apparently not related to investigations into allegations that top police officials had been involved in wiretapping targeting the president.

articles.title: Russian federation head Tretiak says it will seek compensation if barred from world juniors in Alberta

paras.en: Russian federation head Tretiak says it will seek compensation if barred from world juniors in Alberta
Tretiak: 'move the championship, not hold it at all or impose sanctions on Canada'

Russian hockey federation president Vladislav Tretiak is threatening to seek compensation from Canada and push for the relocation or cancellation of next month's world junior championship in Alberta if Russia is barred from competing.

The warning comes after Ottawa confirmed Wednesday that Russian players would not be permitted to compete, even if they already hold valid Canadian visas, despite last month's Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling ordering Russia's reinstatement to international hockey.

Russia's state news agency TASS reported Thursday that Tretiak told a presidential sports council meeting Russia would also seek compensation from Germany, host of the 2027 men's world championship, if denied participation.
"There are rules: if a team does not take the ice, it receives a forfeit loss and sanctions are imposed," Tretiak told TASS in comments translated from Russian.
"The IIHF has a way out — either allow us to participate or, if we cannot enter Canada, move the championship, not hold it at all or impose sanctions on Canada."

Tretiak, a legendary Soviet goaltender and three-time Olympic gold medallist, also told TASS the Russian federation had asked the International Ice Hockey Federation's ethics council to investigate and punish national federations organizing boycotts of games against Russia.

Russian President Vladimir Putin told the same sports council meeting that national federations were refusing matches against Russian teams under pressure from their governments, according to TASS, which did not identify the countries involved.
Several hockey federations, including Finland, Sweden, Czechia and Norway, have said their teams will refuse to face Russia.

The dispute follows an Oct. 30 ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport ordering the IIHF to allow Russian teams to participate in five international tournaments, beginning with the world juniors in Edmonton and Red Deer on Dec. 26.
Russia and Belarus have been banned from international hockey competition since Russia invaded Ukraine with Belarusian assistance in 2022.
Prime Minister Mark Carney said last week that Russian and Belarusian athletes would not be permitted to represent their countries in Canada as long as the war continues.
The federal government's earlier position allowed individual athletes to compete as neutrals, raising questions about whether a Russian team could participate under a neutral designation.
Secretary of State for Sport Adam van Koeverden clarified Monday that the exemption applied only to individual athletes, not national teams.

In a statement Wednesday, van Koeverden said Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada would assess Russian and Belarusian athletes and officials individually to prevent them from competing at the men's under-20 tournament in Alberta, even if they hold valid Canadian visas.
- Canada's secretary of sport questions Russia competing as neutrals at Alberta world juniors
- Norway says it has been bumped by the IIHF to allow Russia to compete at world juniors in Canada
There are Russian players with valid visas competing in the Canadian Hockey League, the umbrella organization for the country's three major junior hockey leagues.

Russian and Belarusian players were banned from the CHL's import draft from 2022-24 before being allowed back in. According to the CHL, Russia led this year's draft with 32 of the 114 players selected.
The controversy has also thrown Norway's participation into question.
Norway's hockey federation said Sunday the IIHF had informed it that Russia would be added to the world junior tournament at Norway's expense.
Norway qualified for the championship and has said it still hopes to compete.

The IIHF has not formally announced any changes to the tournament field, and its website continues to list Norway among the 10 participating teams. The federation did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the possibility of cancelling or relocating the tournament.
The world junior championship will conclude on Jan. 5.

articles.title: Carney wraps meetings on security, trade with European leaders in Ireland
articles.author: Dylan Robertson

paras.en: Carney wraps meetings on security, trade with European leaders in Ireland
Canada only non-European country at European Political Community summit
Prime Minister Mark Carney heard from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Thursday about the state of negotiations with Russia as the two discussed continental security with European leaders.

"Security guarantees are a European responsibility, with Canada, with the United States. So there are tiers for security guarantees," Carney said in French at the start of the European Political Community summit in Dublin.
The summit is an informal gathering of leaders from around Europe that has occurred every six months since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

For the second time, Canada was the only non-European country represented at the table. Since the last meeting in May in Armenia, Carney and European Union leaders have pitched making Canada an "associate member" of the EU — a title they have yet to define.
Carney told reporters that the summit can help advance his goal of boosting affordability and economic opportunities for Canadians through new partnerships with Europe.

"It delivers opportunity — opportunity for our youth, for our artists, for companies. It will deliver affordability, cutting red tape, more competition in Canada, more goods, more choice and security," he said.
Carney also spoke with his counterparts from Greece and Cyprus, two European Union countries that haven't ratified Canada's decade-old trade deal with the EU.
Both countries have held back for reasons that include questions about protected origins for cheeses — such as whether Canadian-made products can be called feta or halloumi.
Carney is seen during a bilateral meeting with Nikos Christodoulides, president of the Republic of Cyprus, on Thursday. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)
In his meeting with Carney, Cyprus's President Nikos Christodoulides said he is committed to getting the trade deal ratified.

"I want to mention this publicly — we are doing whatever is necessary in order to pass the agreement, free trade agreement between the European Union and Canada, which is very important for both of us," he said.

Christodoulides said the meeting was the first between a Canadian prime minister and a Cypriot president in 80 years. He said it reflects the "pro-European Canadian approach" under Carney's leadership.
Carney spoke briefly with reporters at the start of Thursday's meetings, but most of the plenary was not broadcast. He is expected to give a news conference in the coming days.

The summit's Irish hosts have locked down a section of central Dublin for what they are calling its largest ever gathering of international leaders. Police boats have been patrolling the River Liffey and there is a visible security presence across the city.
Schools, newsrooms and an airline have reported receiving bomb threats, which local authorities have said are not credible.
Zelenskyy briefed more than a dozen leaders, including Carney, at a meeting co-hosted by British Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham, centre left, co-hosted the security meeting of the European Political Community summit with Zelenskyy. (Stefan Rousseau/Pool/The Associated Press)
The Ukrainian leader discussed this week's talks in Abu Dhabi with Russian officials organized by U.S. President Donald Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.
The two are set to arrive in Dublin on Thursday evening to speak with Zelenskyy, following a talk earlier in the day in Moscow with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Carney is set to leave for Asia on Thursday evening.
He will attend a summit in the Philippines focused on regional issues, followed by the Francophonie summit in Cambodia.
Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, whose minority government was elected on a sovereignist platform, is also expected to attend the Francophonie summit.
St-Pierre Plamondon has said he wants to conduct diplomacy on Quebec's behalf instead of leaving it to the prime minister.
On the sidelines of Thursday's meeting, French President Emmanuel Macron said he looks forward to speaking with all representatives of the Francophonie.
"It is not my place to interfere in Canadian affairs, but rather to continue supporting our shared affinities, including our cultural and linguistic ties," he said in French.
Carney said he did not attend this week's UN Climate Conference in Turkey — better known as COP31 — because the leaders' day fell on Nov. 11.
"It was more important to be at Remembrance Day to honour the women and men of the Canadian Forces who served our country, who stood for democracy, often in Europe," he said.
Carney added that his environment minister will help advance Canadian interests on electrification at COP31, saying it's a major theme of the summit.

articles.title: Sri Lanka: Rights groups sound alarm over proposed anti-terror law

paras.en: For 46-year-old Ganesan (name changed) from Batticaloa in eastern Sri Lanka, any discussion of terrorism brings back memories of his two-year-old daughter, who was killed in the 2019 Easter Sunday attacks. She was one of 270 people who lost their lives in a series of coordinated bombings targeting three churches and three luxury hotels across the island nation.
The attacks were the deadliest in Sri Lanka since the end of its civil war in 2009. More than 500 people were injured.
Ganesan's daughter was killed in an attack on the Zion Church in Batticaloa.
But Ganesan remains skeptical when asked about the new counterterrorism bill pushed by the government in Sri Lanka.
"Laws against terrorism are necessary to prevent terrorist attacks, but they should not target the innocent or suppress human rights," he told DW.
The administration led by President Anura Kumara Dissanayake and his National People's Power faction

has proposed the Protection of the State from Terrorism Act (PSTA) as a replacement for the existing Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA). The PTA has many critics who claim that the contentious law has enabled arbitrary detention and the torture of detainees for decades.
The government argues that a robust anti-terrorism law is needed to address the increasingly complex local and international activities of extremist groups.
What do rights groups say about the new bill?

Rights groups are now also sharply criticizing the new bill. Activist argue that the changes will not bring about any improvement, warning that the draft features an overly broad definition of terrorism, provides inadequate judicial oversight, and grants extensive powers to law enforcement authorities. Activists also warn that the proposed law has only limited safeguards against official abuse.

The bill, for instance, allows security forces to stop, search and question individuals on the basis of "reasonable suspicion," enter and search premises, and seize items on suspicion of them being linked to an offense under the terrorism act.

"The definition of the term 'terrorism' in the bill as presently drafted is highly problematic. The term is unclear, and its meaning has not been clearly defined," Visakesa Chandrasekaram, a film director and human rights lawyer, told DW.
"Such lack of clarity in the law may result in violations of the fundamental rights of the people," he added.

Chandrasekaram also pointed out that the bill would confer police powers on the military, which is neither trained to investigate criminal offenses nor equipped to protect the rights of people targeted in such investigations.
This, he warned, could lead to the "militarization" of the law enforcement process.
Dhanushka Silva, a lawyer, said the proposed law is not much different from the existing one.
"The present government pledged to repeal the PTA in their 2024 election manifesto. But now the government seems to replace it with a new act that is a replica of the PTA," he told DW.
Silva believes the new bill, PSTA, could be misused to suppress democratic freedoms and muzzle dissent and free speech.
Under Section 9 of the PSTA, even posts or statements made on social media could be subject to scrutiny due to the broad definition of terrorism-related offenses in the bill, he explained.
The section further suggests that individuals who share content deemed to be a terrorism offense could face up to 15 years of rigorous imprisonment, according to the the lawyer.
"This is a big blow to freedom of speech in a democratic society like ours," he said.
The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) has also called on the government to ensure that the bill is consistent with international human rights law.
It noted that the PSTA, despite containing some additional safeguards and improvements on previous drafts, reproduces a number of shortcomings in the PTA and other, older counter-terrorism bills.
The legislation "should include robust safeguards against torture, ill-treatment, enforced disappearance and coercive interrogation," OHCHR said in a statement.
Government spokesperson Nalinda Jayatissa, however, rejected the allegations by rights activists and insisted that the new law would not compromise civil liberties and press freedom.
Calls for Colombo to uphold human rights commitments
Passing the new counterterrorism legislation could also have economic and foreign policy ramifications for Sri Lanka.
The United Nations, which has repeatedly urged Colombo to repeal the PTA, has called for further revisions to the proposed PSTA.

The European Union has likewise urged Sri Lanka to uphold its international human rights obligations if it wishes to continue benefiting from the bloc's Generalized Scheme of Preferences Plus (GSP+), which grants preferential access to the EU market to eligible developing countries.
Failure to meet these requirements could result in the suspension of GSP+ preferences, likely to trigger significant economic penalties for the country.
During a parliamentary debate on November 12, Speaker Jagath Wickramaratne said that some provisions of the proposed law were inconsistent with the constitution.
The legislation was also challenged before the Supreme Court, which outlined several amendments and said Parliament could pass the measure once the changes were made.
Parliament has yet to set a date for a vote.

articles.title: Hungary eases abortion restrictions in women's rights overhaul

paras.en: Hungary on Thursday said it would ease abortion rules and ratify an international treaty on violence against women.
Under the planned changes to the so-called "heartbeat regulation," women will no longer be forced to listen to the vital signs of the fetus before an abortion.
Women will also be able to get emergency contraceptive pills without prescription.
The changes proposed by the new government under Prime Minister Peter Magyar are a significant break with the conservative policies of his predecessor Viktor Orban.
The country also plans to ratify the Istanbul Convention, a treaty aimed at preventing violence against women and domestic violence.
Hungary to end controversial 'fetal heartbeat' policy

Hungarian law allows for most abortions to be performed up to 12 weeks, and up to 24 weeks in cases of severe developmental abnormalities. Until now, women were required to have a medical provider show them evidence of a definitive sign of fetal life, commonly understood as the so-called "fetal heartbeat," before deciding whether to have an abortion.
The controversial 2022 policy had received widespread criticism from doctors and women’s rights groups as being cruel and humiliating. It will now be scrapped.
The policy had not led to a decline in abortions and according to Magyar, had raised "serious bioethical questions."
The second major change is that emergency contraception will be available without prescription.

Further measures include changing the criminal code aimed at better protecting women, including making the misuse of intimate images a criminal offense and strengthening the treatment of victims of domestic violence during criminal proceedings.

Hungary also plans to ratify an international treaty on the protection of women which most other EU members have long ratified. The Istanbul Convention came into force in 2014 and, among other things, requires rape to be criminalized based on the absence of freely given consent.
"We are making it clear that sexual acts can only take place with the voluntary consent of the other party," Magyar said.
The government of his predecessor Orban had opposed the treaty, arguing that it promoted what it described as "gender ideology."
"We are making a clear and accountable commitment to putting an end to the era of inaction," Magyar said in a Facebook video.
Among the EU’s other members, only Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Lithuania and Slovakia have not yet ratified the convention.

The Istanbul Convention is a treaty by the Council of Europe, an international organization that promotes human rights and the rule of law across Europe and includes more countries than the member of the EU.

articles.title: EU leaders tussle over whom to send to Ukraine, Russia peace talks

paras.en: European leaders are under pressure to put forward a name to represent them in Ukraine peace talks after US envoy Steve Witkoff told reporters that the Europeans will be present at the next meetings.

When asked by DW during the European Political Community summit in Dublin why Europe should only get one seat at the table while the US gets two, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas responded with a wry, ironic laugh ― clearly a sign of the frustration felt by European leaders about being sidelined thus far.

The summit of 47 European leaders in Dublin comes in the wake of a diplomatic tour by two Donald Trump administration advisers, the president's son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, to talks in Abu Dhabi, followed by a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.
The pair then hot-footed their way to Dublin to debrief Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelekenskyy.
Zelenskyy and Kushner also said Thursday that Europeans would be at the table for the next talks with Russia on ending the war.

Kallas is one of the figures tipped as most likely to represent the EU in any future talks to end Russia's war against Ukraine, alongside EU Council President Antonio Costa. As yet, the EU hasn’t been able to land on one central figure to send ― many of the national leaders want to be present themselves.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz insisted Europe will be present.
"At the table must be sitting Ukraine, must be sitting the Europeans, must be sitting the Americans, and naturally Russia," he told reporters in Dublin.
But he, like many other leaders, played down the idea of appointing a special envoy for the talks.
Zelenskyy is insistent on European involvement in the peace talks.

"Not directly yet, and not yet when the Russians are at the table," he told the other leaders during the Dublin meetings. "But Europeans are already involved. And we need to make sure that Europe becomes a regular part of these negotiations."

Europe’s division over exactly who should be present has caused a public battle to erupt. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote an excoriating letter to Costa last week, bemoaning the lack of unity.
"By projecting the image of a Europe that is in disarray, we are merely serving the interests of those who want this war to continue," wrote Meloni.
European leaders had even seemed divided over their level of frustration about the situation.

Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Jansa said in Dublin that it was creating a "bad mood" among leaders, however Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs disputed those comments saying, "I don’t feel that."

The palpable fear among the leaders in Dublin is that the US will accept Russia's demands that Europe changes the way it structures its own security, mainly through the NATO military alliance, in exchange for a seat at the table.
Putin said a commitment that Ukraine will never join NATO and even the potential rolling back of the alliance to remove new joiners Finland and Sweden, could be among his demands.

"What do we hear from them [Europeans]?" asked Putin during the meeting with Kushner and Witkoff in Moscow. "That once a peace agreement is signed, they will immediately deploy troops in Ukraine. This is a legitimate target for us, so the war will resume immediately."
This is exactly the kind of rhetoric the European leaders say they are most wary of, especially those in Russia’s direct neighborhood.
"Right now, we are in the [Russian] trap," said Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal. "If something is a threat to you, will you discuss your defense with the threat [itself]?"
US President Donald Trump said publicly that he was hoping for a "very big, beautiful agreement" that "might involve all of Europe."
Zelensky said he found the US approach "a bit strange."
Many of Europe's leaders speaking in Dublin referenced previous agreements with Russia that they believe Moscow has breached.

They include the 1975 Helsinki Accords, the 1990 Paris Charter, 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act and the one they consider most important: the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, which forbids Russia from using force against Ukraine unless in self-defense.
The rancor over the seat at the peace talks is drawing focus away from arguably the bigger battle in the EU now ― how to fund Ukraine as the war continues.
Back in October, the European Commission identified a €70 billion hole in the EU’s funding it had promised for Ukraine’s economy.
Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico has opposed any further financial and military support for Ukraine.
But Germany's Merz warned he could block the EU's next seven-year budget unless member states agree to contribute to Ukraine's financing.

articles.title: Burkina Faso’s rival armed groups turn on each other as state loses ground

paras.en: Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso – Armed fighters from two rival groups have fought a series of increasingly deadly battles along Burkina Faso’s northern border with Mali, as the government struggles to reassert control over large parts of the country.

The clashes between Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM), an al-Qaeda affiliate, and the ISIL affiliate in Sahel Province (ISSP) have intensified since early September, with both groups competing for territory and influence across the borderlands. Their latest confrontations have produced competing claims of heavy casualties, although the figures released by the ISIL (ISIS) group remain unverified.

One of the first major confrontations took place near Kacham, close to the Mali border, in early September. ISSP claimed to have killed more than 200 JNIM fighters, captured more than 30 others and seized weapons and motorcycles. The claim has not been independently verified. Heni Nsaibia, of the monitoring group Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED), said that, if confirmed, the reported death toll would make it the deadliest battle recorded between the two groups.

The fighting escalated again on October 9 around Ganadaouri, in Burkina Faso’s northern Oudalan province. ISIL’s weekly publication, Al-Naba, subsequently claimed that more than 400 JNIM fighters had been killed. JNIM has not publicly responded to the claim, and no independent assessment has established the number of casualties.
The scale of the claim came under further scrutiny when ISSP published photographs on November 1 presented as evidence of its victory, showing what it described as the aftermath of the battle.

Regional news outlet i-Sahel counted at least 120 bodies in the images but said it could not independently verify whether those pictured were victims of the reported fighting. The number visible in the photos is considerably below the 400 deaths claimed by ISIL.
A rivalry that is becoming increasingly costly

The confrontation is part of a rivalry that has persisted since 2019, when the two groups began fighting over territory, influence and access to local populations across the Sahel. Their competition has become increasingly costly, with ACLED recording around 320 armed confrontations between them and more than 2,200 fighter deaths since the conflict began.

The fighting comes as JNIM continues to make gains against government forces in Burkina Faso. The International Crisis Group says the group holds extensive areas of the country, particularly in the north, north-central region, west and east. Its influence has allowed it to challenge state authority across several regions while maintaining operations in neighbouring Mali and Niger.
ACLED’s March 2026 overview documented more than 30 JNIM attacks in Burkina Faso during a February offensive against the military and state-backed Volunteers for the Defense of the Homeland (VDP).

The attacks resulted in the deaths of more than 120 soldiers, forest guards and militia fighters, according to the conflict monitor. The campaign illustrated the pressure facing government forces, even as JNIM had to contend with attacks from its Islamic State rival.
The rivalry could offer Burkina Faso’s authorities some breathing room if JNIM is forced to divert fighters and resources to defend its positions against ISSP.

But there is little reason to assume that the infighting will translate into lasting gains for the government. JNIM remains active across several countries, while ISSP’s battlefield successes could strengthen its position in areas where the two groups compete.
The government faces a wider security crisis

For communities caught between the armed groups and government forces, the prospect of one organisation weakening another offers little certainty of relief. Burkina Faso’s security crisis has displaced millions of people and disrupted access to farmland, markets and basic services.

The scale of the humanitarian crisis remains severe. An estimated 4.5 million people in Burkina Faso need humanitarian assistance in 2026, according to United Nations humanitarian planning figures. The last consolidated official estimate of internal displacement, published in March 2023, put the number at approximately 2.1 million. That figure should not be mistaken for a newly verified 2026 count.

A citizen of Niger, who spoke to Al Jazeera on condition of anonymity because of security concerns, said the fighting between the two groups had raised hopes that communities in the borderlands might face less pressure.

“In Tillaberi, where I have family members, our people have endured too much fear. If JNIM and ISSP keep fighting each other, the danger to our communities may lessen, since their forces may weaken. People here deserve the chance to work their fields, travel safely, and raise their children without fearing attacks from either group.”

The rivalry is no longer confined to Burkina Faso and Mali. ACLED has documented its spread into Niger’s Tillaberi and Dosso regions and Nigeria’s Kebbi State, adding to concerns that the conflict is reaching further into West Africa.
The conflict monitor recorded more than 10,000 deaths from political violence across Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger between January 1 and November 28, 2025.
JNIM’s expansion raises concern across West Africa

Viraj Pattni, a senior associate at Castor Vali, a security risk management company, told Al Jazeera that JNIM’s expanding operations in the region could increase the threat to countries along the Gulf of Guinea.

“The threat of Islamist militancy spreading to coastal countries is very real,” Pattni explained. “Over the past 24 months, JNIM in particular has expanded the intensity of their operations in western and southern Mali. The group has established at least one training camp in the Sikasso Region of Mali, meaning they are well-positioned to continue building their fighting capacity along the border with Ivory Coast.”

“Although the group’s activity isn’t as pronounced in southern regions of Burkina Faso, the epicentre of Islamist militancy in the region, their stranglehold over the Est Region enabled the group to expand and intensify their operations in Togo and Benin in 2025,” he said.
“The group’s activity extended noticeably further into Benin in 2025, and they also claimed their first official attack in Nigeria’s Kwara State in October 2025,” Pattni added.

“Over the longer term, several underlying factors contribute to their likely continued expansion into littoral West Africa, such as porous borders, high levels of marginalisation in northern regions of littoral West African countries and communal tensions, particularly anti-Fulani sentiment.”
ISSP puts pressure on JNIM’s regional dominance

For Nsaibia, of conflict monitor ACLED, the growing confrontation between the two groups could force JNIM to reconsider how it allocates its resources across the region. He said the group had struggled to counter ISSP, which had repeatedly emerged victorious from some of their most significant battles in recent years.

“These increasingly deadly confrontations are forcing JNIM to divert fighters and resources from its primary objective of fighting government forces and allied militias in Mali and Burkina Faso,” Nsaibia said.

articles.title: Harry Kane breaks caps record as England reach Nations League knockouts

paras.en: Harry Kane celebrated his record-breaking 126th England cap with a goal from the penalty spot as England beat Croatia 2-1 on Thursday to book a place in the Nations League quarterfinals.
Slaven Bilic’s team were determined to avoid another embarrassment after their 7-0 mauling by England in Rijeka last month and looked much more solid from the kickoff at Wembley.
But goals from Morgan Rogers and captain Kane kept England second in Group A3 behind Spain, confirming their place in the Nations League last eight in March.
Thomas Tuchel’s men have a chance to avenge their 3-2 defeat against the world champions in their Nations League opener when they travel to Madrid for Sunday’s clash.
Spain beat Czechia 2-0 in Prague on Thursday.
“After the first game when we lost here against them [Spain], we knew we left a bit out there,” Kane told ITV.
“We knew we could’ve done a bit better. We said to ourselves, ‘Let’s win every game until the next one and see what happens’. It’s the perfect opportunity now on Sunday to try and prove ourselves.”
England and Croatia struggled to get out of second gear in the opening stages of their match in London.
Elliot Anderson fired over in the 16th minute, and Croatia’s Josip Misic flashed a shot wide midway through the first half.
Chelsea forward Rogers broke the deadlock in the 24th minute in slightly fortuitous fashion, following a neat move by the home side.
Kane floated a ball to Jude Bellingham on the right of the penalty area and the Real Madrid man cushioned the ball the first time across the area towards Rogers.
Manchester City’s Josko Gvardiol had a chance to clear but got in a tangle and Chelsea’s Rogers poked the ball past goalkeeper Dominik Livakovic.
England started to find some rhythm as they went in search of a second goal but failed to add to their tally before half-time.
The home side were again the more potent team at the beginning of the second period.

But the visitors levelled against the run of play just before the hour mark after a glaring error by England defender Jarell Quansah, who misdirected a header from close range towards Jordan Pickford following a Croatia corner.
The ball fell to Petar Sucic, who stabbed home.
Minutes later England were back in front, with Bayer Leverkusen defender Quansah again at the heart of the action after his shirt was tugged in the penalty area.
Referee Morten Krogh initially did not award a penalty, but he was sent to the monitor by the VAR and pointed to the spot.
Kane made no mistake, drilling home for a record-extending 92nd England goal.
Nikola Vlasic gave England a scare, firing just wide of Jordan Pickford’s goal as Croatia showed they were still alive.
James Garner thought he had scored a third for England after a Bellingham cut-back, but Bellingham was in an offside position when he received the ball.
Ballon d’Or winner Kane won his 126th cap when the game kicked off, taking him clear of his tie with former goalkeeper Peter Shilton.
A giant banner was raised before kickoff with a picture of the 33-year-old and the words “England’s Finest”.
Shilton was part of a pre-match presentation to honour the Three Lions skipper, along with Football Association patron Prince William.

articles.title: Australia captain Pat Cummins denies involvement in ‘Sandpapergate’ scandal

paras.en: Australia captain Pat Cummins has again denied any involvement in the plot to use sandpaper on the ball in a Test against South Africa in 2018, describing the allegations in Usman Khawaja’s autobiography as “utter nonsense”.

Former Australia batsman Khawaja, whose autobiography was published on Tuesday, said last weekend that all the players in the team knew about the plot to rough up the ball with sandpaper to make it swing. His latest comments triggered calls for a new investigation into the incident.
The scandal centred around the third Test in Cape Town, but Khawaja also claimed the tactic was used in the second Test at Port Elizabeth.

“When he says we all knew, if by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out in the field, he’s 100 percent wrong. I’ve said that consistently for the last eight years,” Cummins told a news conference in Sydney on Friday.
“I did not know that was happening, but I think Usman actually says things that are actually far more serious than that.
“He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper. That’s complete and utter nonsense.
“There was no master plan around using illegal methods,” he added. “There’s no grand plan. There’s no team meeting. There’s no bowlers saying ‘this is what must happen’.”
Cummins and fellow bowlers Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon all denied publicly in a 2021 statement that they were aware of the plan.
Darren Lehmann, who was the Australian head coach at the time, has also denied any knowledge, as has former batting coach Graeme Hick, who called Khawaja’s allegations “absolutely false”.
Cummins spoke for 68 minutes on Friday, taking every question from the media and saying he would never discuss the ball-tampering incident again.
The Australia skipper also took exception to Pakistan-born Khawaja’s contention in the book that the colour of his skin and background had prevented him from becoming Australia captain.
“I think of all the things that I’ve read this week, I think that’s actually the most serious,” he said.
“Him saying that if you’re Australian captain, you have to be a certain skin colour, I couldn’t disagree with that statement any more.”
Steve Smith and David Warner, the then-Australia captain and vice-captain, were banned by Cricket Australia from elite cricket for a year for their roles in the ball-tampering.
Opening batter Cameron Bancroft, who brought a piece of sandpaper onto the field, received a nine-month suspension for his part in the ball-tampering.
“I was genuinely shocked this week when I found out that Usman admitted that he told Cam to be careful when using sandpaper. That’s not the Usman that I know,” Cummins said.
“It’s not the Usman that has helped rebuild the Australian cricket culture over the last eight years.”
Later on Friday, Warner said the trio had paid a heavy price for the incident and revealed that his wife Candice had lost a baby in the aftermath of what became known as “Sandpapergate“.
“I still stick by Uzzie and what he has written in that book. It is the truth,” the former Test opener said in TV commentary ahead of a one-day international between Australia and England.
“I actually feel for [Khawaja] at the moment. I actually feel that the captain today threw Uzzie under the bus and I’m very disappointed by that.”
Cummins was asked about Khawaja’s recollection that two players had rejected the batsman’s call for the team to take collective responsibility for the ball-tampering.
“I don’t remember any conversation around collective responsibility,” he said.
“So then, I’ve got no idea who those two people would be because I don’t remember ever being asked or having a conversation about it.”
Khawaja and Warner have also been critical of the Cricket Australia investigation in 2018 that found the three punished players solely responsible for the plot.
“I got asked to be part of that review,” Cummins said. “I was totally truthful. I’ve been very consistent since then at that event till now. Nothing’s changed.”
Earlier this week, the head of Cricket Australia ruled out opening another investigation into the 2018 incident.
Cummins said he respected the right of Khawaja to tell his story in the autobiography but felt some of the allegations were very serious and had to be addressed.
“Usman’s a friend, but friends aren’t casual with each other’s lives and reputations,” he said.
“In his book, Uzzie has been casual with my life and the lives of many others, and I think Australian cricket.”
Cummins added, though, that he would not be taking legal action against Khawaja over the allegations in the book.
“I did get advised this week that some of the things that’ve been said are probably defamatory, but I won’t be doing that,” Cummins said.
“You’ve got to move on. It’s been eight years. We’re moving on. So, you got to draw a line at some point.”

articles.title: U.S. officials set to meet with Putin, Zelenskyy following Abu Dhabi peace talks
articles.author: Charles Maynes

paras.en: U.S. officials set to meet with Putin, Zelenskyy following Abu Dhabi peace talks
U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi have wrapped up with an agreement on a Russia-Ukraine prisoner exchange. U.S. negotiators meet with Vladimir Putin on Thursday and Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday.
President Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are in Moscow today for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Then they'll move on to Europe to meet with Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. And their goal will be to see if they can make more headway on U.S. efforts to end Russia's war with Ukraine following two days of talks between the two sides in Abu Dhabi.
MARTIN: NPR's Charles Maynes is in Moscow to tell us more. Good morning, Charles.
CHARLES MAYNES, BYLINE: Morning, Michel.
MARTIN: So let's start with these peace talks in Abu Dhabi. Did they achieve anything?

MAYNES: Well, these negotiations were the first since February, and they delivered just one concrete result. Russia and Ukraine agreed to what's been billed as the largest prisoner exchange so far in the war. That's, of course, good news, but it's not why the U.S. got these two sides together. The goal here was and is much bigger.

MAYNES: Well, the U.S. entered into these talks saying it wanted to explore a new long-term security arrangement between Russia and Europe, believing that that could unlock concessions from both Kyiv and Moscow to end the actual fighting. And so that really was the focus in Abu Dhabi, all the more so because negotiations over ceasefires and other concessions have really gone nowhere, as Kushner noted after the talks.
JARED KUSHNER: The reality is there's no trust right now between the sides, and that's to be expected after a conflict like this.
MAYNES: So he's really just trying something new.
MARTIN: And do we have a sense of how Russia's responding to all this?

MAYNES: Well, this is a conversation the Kremlin has been demanding because, at least from President Putin's perspective, the war in Ukraine has always been about relitigating the end of the Cold War. It's about establishing buffer zones against NATO's expansion, and that really means a new approach to European security. Russia's lead negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, in Abu Dhabi used this rather colorful metaphor.

MAYNES: So here he says that the whole body of European security is sick and needs curing, and calling Ukraine a cyst that had burst to the point where a Band-Aid wouldn't help. Now, Medinsky went on to add that in some areas, Russia and the U.S. had found some common ground. Clearly, it didn't include territorial concessions. After the talks, he told Russian media that, quote, "every inch of our land" would be returned one way or another, so not exactly signaling flexibility.
MARTIN: And what are the Ukrainians saying to all this?

MAYNES: Well, they were upbeat because in these conversations is something Ukraine's also been after - security guarantees against any future Russian incursion, although we don't have details. What we do know is that going into these talks, U.S. officials were exploring Article 5-like guarantees for Ukraine from the U.S. That's a reference to NATO's collective security defense, which, if it happened, would be a huge deal. The catch - Moscow's already rejected the idea of a NATO-like status for Ukraine, just as it rejects Ukraine's full membership in the alliance.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: MARTIN: OK. So let's turn to the Moscow visit. What exactly are Witkoff and Kushner hoping to do?

MAYNES: Well, Kushner said they want to brief Putin directly and convince him to include Europeans in these discussions, which are, after all, about European security. Now, European governments are clearly nervous about a deal being cut with Moscow over their heads, so much so they sent envoys to Abu Dhabi to get updates from the U.S. and Ukraine on the sidelines. And some European leaders are expected to join Kushner and Witkoff when they meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Ireland. That's likely to happen tomorrow. But Russia's been really dismissive about the idea, given Europe's military support for Ukraine. How dismissive? Well, Medinsky, the head of the Russian delegation, compared the Europeans in Abu Dhabi to tourists hanging out in the hotel lobby.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: MARTIN: Wow. That's NPR's Charles Maynes in Moscow. Charles, thank you.

articles.title: Former U.S. Ambassador William Taylor discusses the latest Russia-Ukraine talks
articles.author: A Martínez

paras.en: Former U.S. Ambassador William Taylor discusses the latest Russia-Ukraine talks
NPR's A Martinez speaks with former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine, William Taylor, about the ongoing peace talks between the U.S., Russia and Ukraine.

William Taylor has been listening along with us. He served as U.S. ambassador to Ukraine during the George W. Bush and Obama administrations. Ambassador, so I know no major breakthroughs, but a prisoner swap. So is this an accomplishment, nonetheless?

WILLIAM TAYLOR: Not that great, A. Of course, it's good to have prisoners come back. That's always a good thing. But what they're really after is ending the war. They want a ceasefire. And they apparently made no progress toward that.

MARTÍNEZ: OK. Now, one of the biggest sticking points in these negotiations is the role of Europe, or what role Europe may play in all of this going forward. Moscow doesn't want Europe involved. Meanwhile Europe is focusing on protecting the continent from Russian aggression, any future Russian aggression. So in your view, should Europe be involved somehow in these direct talks?

TAYLOR: Absolutely. Absolutely. Not only indirectly, they should be directly there. They should be at the table. As you say, this is about European security. But it's first about supporting Ukraine and allowing them to prevail. And the Europeans have been there, more so now, A, than the Americans. So the Europeans should definitely be there. They have a lot at stake, and they're a strong supporter of Ukraine.
MARTÍNEZ: If European involvement, though, is something Vladimir Putin draws a line in the sand on, how does that happen then?

TAYLOR: Then the Ukrainians say no. The Ukrainians say, no, we don't have the conversation unless the Europeans are there. And the Americans are also there. The U.S. position is Europeans need to be there. That will be the message, the combined message, to the Russians.
MARTÍNEZ: Yeah. It sounds like Jared Kushner has an almost impossible task here, doing something that I think he wants to do but Vladimir Putin obviously doesn't, to bring Europe in these talks.

TAYLOR: So Kushner and Witkoff have a flawed way of thinking about these negotiations. They think that if they just offer suggestions or offerings or carrots or gifts to Putin, he'll come around to their point of view. That's wrong, A. As you know, Putin responds to strength, not to gifts. And so that's not going to get them anywhere.
MARTÍNEZ: But strength, that could be something that is dangerous to the world, isn't it? Showing a force of strength to Vladimir Putin sounds like it could be dangerous to everyone.

TAYLOR: It's going to be dangerous to the Russians if they continue. The Russians know - Putin knows that if he lashes out at anybody in NATO, it's curtains for him. There is no way that the Russians are going to go after NATO. So NATO needs to be strong, Europeans need to be strong, Ukrainians are strong and the U.S. should be supportive.

MARTÍNEZ: Ambassador, I remember back in 2022, Vladimir Putin expected this so-called special military operation to last anywhere from three to 10 days, or weeks at worst. Come February, it'll be five years. What are the chances that Vladimir Putin can be convinced that maybe he cannot win this war?

TAYLOR: He's going to come to that conclusion, A. I'm convinced. He sees the refineries that are burning in his country. The Ukrainians are going deep after them. I don't know if his generals are telling him, but he's losing 50,000 troops in a month. That can't go on. You know, when Putin understands that, he will figure this out. The U.S. elections, A, are going to be a message to him that says the U.S. is supportive of Ukraine. Three percent of Americans support Russia. This is going to become clear to him that he cannot win this.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: MARTÍNEZ: You think he will arrive to that conclusion, or someone has to pressure him or convince him to arrive there?

TAYLOR: I think someone has to pressure him to convince him. The Ukrainians are doing that on the battlefield. John Ratcliffe, you recall, the head of the CIA, went to Moscow to try to tell Putin this. Putin wouldn't listen, but he's hearing it from his generals.
MARTÍNEZ: All right. William Taylor is a former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine, now with the Atlantic Council. Ambassador, thank you very much.

articles.title: Former Ukrainian foreign minister discusses how to bridge gaps between Ukraine, Russia
articles.author: A Martínez

paras.en: Former Ukrainian foreign minister discusses how to bridge gaps between Ukraine, Russia
NPR's A Martinez asks Ukraine's former Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba for his proposals to close gaps in talks between Russia, Ukraine and Europe.

Let's hear from a former Ukrainian official with extensive experience negotiating on behalf of the country. Dmytro Kuleba was foreign minister for Ukraine from 2020 to 2024. Today, he's a senior fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School's Belfer Center. Minister, Russia and Ukraine agreed, at least in principle, to a large-scale prisoner exchange as part of these talks. They've done that before. Were you hoping for more progress to be made with these talks?

DMYTRO KULEBA: No, I didn't. And I actually have to say that prisoner swaps should be taking place outside of the scope of political negotiations as a part of regular humanitarian effort. But I don't see any driver behind Russia's position that has changed recently in the trajectory of genuine negotiations in good faith.
MARTÍNEZ: So as far as making progress toward ending the war, these prisoner exchanges to you means nothing?

KULEBA: Well, prisoners exchange means the world to every Ukrainian because our people are coming back home to their family from Russian prisons, where they're subjected to torture and disregarding treatment. So it's a big deal. But it has zero impact on the progress on the political track towards ending the conflict.

MARTÍNEZ: When it comes to Europe's role in these talks, we know that Vladimir Putin does not want Europe involved. And the U.S. has said that NATO allies are essential to a lasting peace. Is there a way for U.S. envoys to persuade Russia, to persuade Vladimir Putin to accept European involvement in these talks?
MARTÍNEZ: If European presence in these talks doesn't cost Russia anything, why doesn't the U.S. basically just hold Vladimir Putin's hands to the fire on this and insist on them being there?
KULEBA: Could you give me one example from the last two years when the United States held President Putin's arms to the fire?
KULEBA: That's not the way this administration treats President Putin. They actually more kind of care for his hands than want to cause harm to them.

MARTÍNEZ: So if you know that, minister - and obviously, Vladimir Putin probably knows that - then what are the chances that any progress can be made? All he has to do is just continue to hold the line.

KULEBA: Well, that's exactly what he has been doing for the last two years. And this is what I believe, regrettably, he will continue to do in the coming years. He just needs to continue engaging with his - engage the United States, court President Trump in a way that will give him enough of a reason to believe that an agreement is possible, and that Putin is seeking an agreement but just needs to be accommodated on one or two more points.
MARTÍNEZ: Do you think that Democratic control of the new Congress, the upcoming Congress, will somehow alter the course of these talks or maybe the future of U.S. support for Ukraine?

KULEBA: Well, foreign policy, especially in negotiations with foreign leaders, stays firmly in the hands of the president of the United States of America. So, yes, of course I expect a reinvigorated role of Congress on the Ukrainian file. But I believe President Trump will continue his policies.
MARTÍNEZ: Dmytro Kuleba served as Ukraine's foreign minister from 2020 to 2024. He's now at the Harvard Kennedy School's Belfer Center. Minister, thank you very much for your time.
(SOUNDBITE OF MICK TURNER, TREN BROTHERS AND JIM WHITE'S "JENNY'S SONG")
