articles.title: A massive new simulation reveals how the universe emerged from darkness

paras.en: A massive new simulation reveals how the universe emerged from darkness
A massive new supercomputer simulation reveals how the first stars, galaxies, and black holes helped bring the universe out of its cosmic dark age.

- A groundbreaking new supercomputer simulation is revealing how the universe escaped its cosmic dark age and transformed into a cosmos filled with stars and galaxies. Called Lumina, it recreates 2 billion years of early cosmic history across a region 1.6 billion light-years wide, capturing extraordinary details that previous simulations could not.

A powerful new computer simulation is allowing scientists to explore one of the most mysterious periods in cosmic history, when the universe emerged from darkness and the first stars and galaxies began to transform the cosmos.

Developed by researchers at MIT, Harvard University, and other institutions, the simulation, called Lumina, recreates the evolution of the early universe across a region roughly 1.6 billion light-years wide. It follows 2 billion years of cosmic history, revealing how galaxies formed, how radiation spread through space, and how the universe gradually became transparent to light.

The research, published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS), provides an unusually detailed picture of events that unfolded billions of years before our solar system existed.
How the Universe Entered Its Cosmic Dark Age

The story begins with the Big Bang, when the universe existed in an extremely hot, dense state filled with electrons and other subatomic particles. This primordial plasma, described as initially smaller than a single atom, expanded rapidly and cooled as the universe grew.

Eventually, particles slowed enough for electrons to combine with atomic nuclei, producing electrically neutral hydrogen. Around 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the universe entered a period known as the cosmic "dark age."

Although the universe had become transparent to much of the radiation left over from the Big Bang, stars had not yet formed to illuminate the cosmos. Neutral hydrogen filled space and could absorb certain types of radiation, including the ultraviolet light that would later emerge from the first stars.
Lumina allows researchers to investigate how this early environment evolved, eventually giving rise to the galaxies, stars, and other structures that helped bring the dark age to an end.
How the First Stars and Black Holes Transformed the Universe

The simulation covers an immense region measuring 500 megaparsecs, equivalent to approximately 1.6 billion light-years. Within that volume, Lumina follows dark matter, gas, stars, and radiation (such as photons), capturing both the behavior of matter across enormous distances and the formation of individual galaxies.
One of its most important achievements is recreating two major changes in the early universe: hydrogen re-ionization and helium re-ionization.

Hydrogen re-ionization began as the first stars and galaxies produced increasing amounts of ultraviolet radiation. This energetic light removed electrons from neutral hydrogen atoms, a process called "re-ionizing" the gas. As more hydrogen became ionized, the universe became increasingly transparent to ultraviolet light, allowing radiation to travel across much greater distances.

This transformation helped clear the widespread neutral hydrogen that had dominated the early cosmos. Lumina reproduces the process in remarkable detail, showing how radiation from the first generations of stars gradually changed the conditions throughout space.
The simulation also follows helium re-ionization, which requires substantially more energetic radiation to strip electrons from helium.

The results point to different sources driving these two transformations. Early stars and galaxies appear to have been primarily responsible for ionizing hydrogen, while actively feeding supermassive black holes supplied the intense radiation needed to ionize helium.
This is the first simulation to capture both processes together, offering a more complete view of how the early universe changed.

"Lumina does everything from small-scale star and galaxy formation to large-scale reionization of hydrogen and helium, in a volume that is 100 times larger than previous best simulations," says study author Mark Vogelsberger, a professor of physics at MIT.

The researchers are making Lumina available to other scientists, allowing its predictions about early cosmic structures to be compared with observations from existing and future telescopes. Such comparisons could help researchers better understand the events that shaped the first galaxies and stars.
Building a Virtual Universe With Half a Trillion Elements

Lumina gets its name from the Latin word meaning "lights." Its underlying technology builds on IllustrisTNG, an earlier simulation developed by scientists at MIT and other institutions, including members of the Lumina research team.
IllustrisTNG models how galaxies form and evolve by following the interactions of dark matter, gas, and other physical processes from the Big Bang to the present day.

To create Lumina, researchers upgraded the existing software so it could reproduce galaxy formation in comparable detail across a much larger region of space. They also incorporated a radiation transport model that calculates how light, including ultraviolet radiation, travels through the universe and interacts with surrounding matter.
Together, these improvements allow the simulation to track both the formation of galaxies and the enormous changes that radiation produces across cosmic distances.

The resulting model contains approximately half a trillion individual elements, including particles of dark matter and cells representing gas. It provides roughly 30 times the resolution of IllustrisTNG while covering a region 100 times larger in volume than previous leading simulations.

Recreating billions of years of interactions across so many elements requires extraordinary computing resources. The researchers used Frontier, one of the world's most powerful supercomputers, located at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee.

"At peak scale, the calculation brings together the equivalent of more than 100,000 CPU cores and around 15,000 GPUs," says Xuejian (Jacob) Shen, an MIT co-author of the study. "Making all of those processors communicate efficiently while continuously evolving trillions of interacting pieces of information is itself an extraordinary feat of computer engineering."
Watching the First Galaxies Emerge From Darkness
Lumina begins approximately 45 million years after the Big Bang, during an era when neutral hydrogen dominated the universe.

Researchers initialized the simulation using conditions based on scientists' understanding of that period. They then allowed the model to calculate how gas and dark matter interacted throughout its half a trillion elements as cosmic time progressed.
At the same time, Lumina tracked how radiation appeared, spread, and interacted with matter, including the ultraviolet light produced by emerging stars.

The result is a virtual universe that scientists can explore at dramatically different scales, from the arrangement of matter across enormous cosmic distances down to the development of a single galaxy.

On the project website, the researchers have released videos showing these processes in action. One offers a "zoom-in" from the entire simulated region to an individual disk-shaped galaxy. Another presents a time-lapse of the complete volume, showing how hydrogen re-ionization spreads across the universe over 2 billion years.

"On the one hand, it's evolving dark matter as well as the gas in the universe, and on the other, it's also tracking how radiation travels," Zier explains. "We see dark matter and gas start to clump in these over-densities. And when we zoom in, we can see gas is falling into these dark matter haloes. Zooming in more, we see this is where the first galaxies form. And the first stars form in those first galaxies. Those stars then create radiation. The simulation then tracks that radiation, and we can zoom way out to see how that radiation travels out from stars, through the universe, until at some point it ionizes some neutral hydrogen."

paras.en: This ability to move between vastly different scales is one of Lumina's defining strengths. Researchers can examine the formation of individual galaxies while also observing how their combined radiation affects the universe on a much larger scale.
"Other simulations cannot zoom in as far as this," Vogelsberger notes. "The difference between the smallest and largest scales that we simulate is larger than in any other simulation."
A New Way to Explore the Universe's Earliest History

The research team plans to use Lumina to investigate the large-scale arrangement of matter in the early universe. The simulation could also help predict the patterns of gravitational waves generated by ancient galaxies and black holes.

Another major opportunity will come from comparing Lumina's virtual universe with real observations. New and upcoming telescopes are expected to collect increasingly detailed information about enormous numbers of distant galaxies, providing scientists with fresh ways to test their understanding of the early cosmos.
Because Lumina simulates such a large volume of space, it can generate extensive populations of galaxies that can be directly compared with these observations.

"One of Lumina's major advantages is its sheer size," Shen says. "It produces enormous populations of simulated galaxies, finally allowing us to make comparisons with the very large galaxy samples that upcoming surveys will observe."

By bringing together detailed galaxy formation, dark matter, gas, and the movement of radiation, Lumina offers researchers a powerful new tool for reconstructing the universe's earliest chapters. It may help explain not only how the first galaxies took shape, but also how their stars and black holes transformed the surrounding cosmos.

The study's MIT authors include Mark Vogelsberger, Xuejian (Jacob) Shen, and Teodora-Elena Bluichi. Other contributors include first author Oliver Zier (a former postdoc in the Vogelsberger Lab), Rongrong Liu, Sonja Koehler, and Lars Hernquist of the Harvard and Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics; Aaron Smith of the University of Texas at Dallas; Rahul Kannan of York University in Canada; and Volker Springel and Rüdiger Pakmor of the Max Planck Institute for Astrophysics in Germany.

The research received partial support from NASA and the National Science Foundation. It also used computing resources at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, which is supported by the Advanced Scientific Computing Research programs within the Office of Science at the U.S. Department of Energy.

articles.title: Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread

paras.en: Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread

- Scientists have uncovered a surprising way that fructose, a sugar commonly found in sweetened foods and drinks, may help aggressive ovarian cancer spread. Researchers discovered that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy release fructose that weakens the bonds holding neighboring tumor cells together, making it easier for cancer to spread. High dietary fructose levels and cholesterol-lowering statins also produced concerning effects in preclinical experiments.

A common sugar found in many foods and sweetened drinks may play an unexpected role in helping aggressive ovarian cancer spread. Researchers at The Wistar Institute have discovered that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy can release fructose, which acts as a signal that encourages nearby tumor cells to break free and spread.

The findings, published in Nature Aging, reveal a previously unknown way that cancer cells can continue influencing a tumor even after treatment has stopped them from multiplying. The discovery also raises important questions about whether dietary sugar and commonly prescribed cholesterol medications could affect how cancer progresses.

"Some cancer cells that survive chemotherapy aren't dividing anymore, but they're still biologically active," said Aidan Cole, Ph.D., a postdoctoral fellow in the lab of Katherine Aird, Ph.D., at The Wistar Institute and first author on the study. "Instead, they continue to release molecules that send signals to nearby cells. Our study is among the first to show that a nutrient -- in this case, fructose -- can act as one of those signals."
Why Ovarian Cancer Often Returns After Chemotherapy

Most patients with ovarian cancer receive platinum-based chemotherapy, a treatment that uses drugs containing platinum to damage the DNA of cancer cells and prevent them from reproducing. Although many patients initially respond well, the cancer eventually returns in most cases. It also frequently spreads throughout the abdominal cavity, the space inside the abdomen that contains organs such as the stomach, intestines, and liver.

This spread, known as metastasis, is responsible for approximately 90% of ovarian cancer deaths. Understanding what allows cancer cells to escape from their original location and establish new tumors is therefore a major priority for researchers.

Previous studies have suggested that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy may contribute to recurrence even when they are no longer actively dividing. These surviving cells can continue producing and releasing a mixture of substances that influence the behavior of surrounding cells.

To investigate this process, Cole and his colleagues developed an experiment that separated the surviving cancer cells from the molecules they released. They discovered that these released substances, even without the surviving cells themselves, were enough to significantly increase cancer spread in a preclinical model.

"As far as we know, this is the first time anyone has shown, in a preclinical model rather than just a dish, that it's the molecules these cells release -- not the cells themselves -- that drive the cancer's spread," said Cole.
A Common Sugar Emerges as a Surprising Cancer Signal
The next challenge was identifying which substances were responsible for encouraging cancer cells to spread. The researchers discovered an unexpected culprit: fructose.

Fructose is a naturally occurring sugar found in fruit, honey, and other foods. It is also a component of table sugar and high fructose corn syrup, a sweetener frequently used in soft drinks and processed foods.

The study revealed that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy could produce fructose and release it into their surroundings. Rather than simply serving as an energy source, the sugar acted as a chemical messenger that encouraged neighboring cancer cells to become more capable of spreading.

The researchers also uncovered another concerning possibility. In their preclinical experiments, consuming high amounts of fructose comparable to those found in sugary drinks could promote signals associated with cancer spread even without chemotherapy treatment.

This observation suggests that diet might influence cancer progression through a mechanism scientists had not previously recognized. Fructose consumption is particularly relevant in the United States, where high fructose corn syrup can account for approximately 8% to 20% of daily calorie intake in some individuals.

Unlike many factors that influence cancer risk and progression, dietary fructose intake can be changed. That raises the possibility that nutritional strategies might eventually become part of efforts to limit cancer spread.

However, researchers have not yet tested whether reducing fructose consumption improves outcomes in patients with ovarian cancer. The findings do not establish that eating sugar causes cancer to spread in humans, and additional research is needed before specific dietary recommendations can be made based on this mechanism.
How Fructose Helps Cancer Cells Break Free
To understand how fructose encourages cancer spread, the researchers examined what happens inside cancer cells exposed to the sugar.

They used several advanced methods to investigate the biological changes involved, including a CRISPR screen. This technique allows scientists to systematically examine genes and identify which ones influence a particular cellular process.
The experiments revealed that fructose suppresses cholesterol production in neighboring cancer cells.

Although cholesterol is often discussed in connection with heart disease, it also serves essential functions throughout the body. It is an important component of cell membranes, the thin outer layers that surround cells and help regulate how they interact with their environment.

In this case, cholesterol helps maintain the connections that hold neighboring cells together. These connections act somewhat like biological glue, making it harder for cancer cells to separate from one another.
When fructose reduces cholesterol production, those connections weaken. As a result, cancer cells can detach more easily, potentially allowing them to escape and spread to other locations.
This discovery provides a possible explanation for how a common nutrient can influence one of the most dangerous aspects of cancer.
A Surprising Connection Between Statins and Cancer Spread
The cholesterol finding also led researchers to investigate an unexpected question involving statins, medications widely prescribed to lower cholesterol.

Approximately 39 million people in the United States take statins. These drugs work by reducing the body's production of cholesterol and are commonly used to lower the risk of heart attacks and strokes.
Because fructose appeared to promote cancer spread by suppressing cholesterol production, the research team wanted to know whether statins might produce similar effects.
Their experiments showed that statins alone could weaken the connections between cancer cells, making it easier for them to separate and escape.

The finding raises questions about whether cholesterol-lowering medications could influence the effectiveness of chemotherapy in certain situations. Researchers are now investigating that possibility, but they emphasize that the results have not been demonstrated in patients and are not a reason for anyone to discontinue prescribed statins.

"We haven't tested this effect in patients yet, but it raises questions about combining cholesterol-lowering drugs with chemotherapy, especially since ovarian cancer is most common in postmenopausal women who are often already on statins," said Katherine Aird, Ph.D., professor and co-leader of the Molecular and Cellular Oncogenesis Program in the Ellen and Ronald Caplan Cancer Center at The Wistar Institute, and senior author of the study.
Could Fructose Also Help Other Cancers Spread?
Although the research focused on ovarian cancer, the scientists suspect that the same biological process could occur in other forms of the disease.

Cancers affecting organs within the abdomen and torso can also spread to nearby tissues and organs. If fructose influences the connections between cancer cells in a similar way, the discovery could have implications beyond ovarian cancer.

"We think other cancers that spread within the torso -- pancreatic, colon, liver -- could behave similarly. We can't call it universal yet, but we think the effects are not just limited to ovarian cancer," said Aird.
Aird and Cole have already begun designing additional experiments to determine whether their findings can be reproduced in pancreatic, colon, liver, and other cancers.

The research opens a new avenue for understanding how cancer spreads, particularly after chemotherapy. It also suggests that the relationship between nutrients, cholesterol production, and cancer cell behavior may be more complicated than previously understood.

While the potential implications for diet and medication remain uncertain, identifying fructose as a signal that helps cancer cells break free could eventually point researchers toward new strategies for preventing metastasis and improving cancer treatment.

articles.title: We can't see Fast Radio Bursts but we can now hear them thanks to a Finnish Cathedral
articles.author: Sharmila Kuthunur

paras.en: Fast radio bursts, flashes of energy from faraway galaxies, are invisible to our eyes. However, we can now hear their melody, thanks to a composer who has turned them into sound.

Fast radio bursts, or FRBs, are among the most extreme events in the universe, releasing as much energy in a millisecond as the sun puts out in three days and briefly outshining entire galaxies. Since the first FRB was discovered in 2007, astronomers have detected thousands of them; however, exactly how these cosmic flares are launched remains poorly understood. Recent evidence points to at least one burst coming from the environment around a rotating neutron star.

Despite their power, FRBs last only a few thousandths of a second before vanishing into space. Catching one takes luck, as a telescope has to be pointed at the right patch of sky at the right moment. That changed with CHIME (the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment) in British Columbia. With a very wide field of view and a supercomputer to process its data, CHIME more than quadrupled the number of known FRBs in its first year of operation alone. Between 2018 and 2023, CHIME recorded 4,539 bursts from 3,641 sources.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: As pulses of radio waves, our eyes haven't evolved to see FRBs, nor can we hear them as they aren't sound waves. Well, not until now.

"Artist and composer Andrew Melchior turned all of the CHIME bursts into sound for "The Logos," an installation that has played daily at Oulu Cathedral in Finland since early April and is scheduled to run through the end of the year. Melchior and Kiyoshi Masui, an associate professor of physics at MIT, "sonified" the bursts, translating data into acoustics so that human ears can hear them.

The structure of each real signal is mapped to varying musical pitches and played through 12 loudspeakers spread throughout the cathedral. The result is a range of tones, with distant FRBs humming, rumbling, popping, and whistling.
The signals are old by any human measure. According to a description on Melchior's website, the youngest in the work are about 50 million years old, and the oldest are about 8 to 9 billion years old.

Physics also plays a role in what is heard. Each burst arrives with its high frequencies first and sweeps downward, stretched by its journey through intergalactic gas, "and you can hear that dispersion as it falls from the dome," Melchior told Space.com by email.

Since their discovery in 2007, the bursts are also still yielding discoveries. Last month, astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope pinpointed the host galaxy of the most distant FRB yet, one that went off when the universe was only about 3 billion years old.

The galaxy, a small, young, star-forming dwarf, was far smaller than expected. That makes it harder to square with the theory that FRBs come from merging neutron stars, researchers say, which would take billions of years to occur.
This fits better with a second theory, in which a young, highly magnetic neutron star called a magnetar produces the burst soon after a massive star explodes, according to NASA.

Back on Earth, an upcoming event at Oulu Cathedral offers a more immediate encounter with the bursts. On Nov. 21, 30 singers will stand among the audience and "sing back to the sky in Finnish" while Melchior plays the bursts live from a keyboard, he told Space.com by email.
"The fast flashes will echo as snare-like beats bouncing through the cathedral," Masui said in a previous MIT statement.
"It should feel rich and layered, while also revealing something real about how these signals travel across billions of years of cosmic space before reaching Earth."

Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. Her work has also appeared in Scientific American, Science, Astronomy and Live Science, among other publications. She holds a master's degree in journalism from Northeastern University in Boston.

articles.title: NASA kick-starts a fresh push to bring Mars samples home
articles.author: Leonard David

paras.en: A long-term goal at NASA has been the ability to robotically haul back to Earth specimens from the Red Planet.

NASA is kickstarting a new initiative for its troubled Mars Sample Return (MSR) program, called the Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture, or PSRA in space shorthand. The plan is to establish a fresh NASA strategy for gathering Mars samples collected by the Perseverance rover and launching them back to Earth.
The PSRA initiative was noted on Nov. 9 by Tiffany Morgan, director of the NASA Mars Exploration Program (MEP), during the virtual meeting of the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group (MEPAG).
- Develop impartial recommendations for retrieving the Martian samples collected by NASA's Perseverance Mars rover and deliver them to Earth
- Evaluate current capabilities and acquisition options
Morgan noted that there will be a PSRA strategy team kickoff in January 2027 with a final report due in winter 2027-2028.
The backdrop to the PSRA activity is that there's one busy rover already on the Red Planet snagging and bagging samples.

NASA's Perseverance Mars rover remains on the prowl within Jezero Crater following its touchdown in February 2021. That car-sized robot has been grabbing select specimens from across the area and gingerly dropping the sealed pick-me-ups on the surface of Mars, as well as stuffing them inside the rover itself.
Those collectibles may well hold signs of past life on the enigmatic, dusty and foreboding Red Planet.

NASA and the European Space Agency have for years been intently plotting out plans to send future spacecraft to Mars and haul those Perseverance-plucked bits, pieces, and sniffs of atmosphere to Earth for rigorous inspection here on Earth using state-of-the-art equipment.

However, over the years, multiple reviews of a NASA Mars Sample Return (MSR) project by independent groups have reported sticker shock findings. Indeed, one last price tag came in at about $11 billion, with samples being returned to Earth in 2040. That finding was deemed by NASA itself as too costly and not doable within an acceptable time frame.
Yet another appraisal group ended up finding it feasible to return Mars samples as early as 2035 for a less costly ship and shoot cost of some $8 billion.
How the PSRA review deals with MSR cost and a multitude of other concerns is in the to-be-determined column.
In the first place, why are samples from Mars delivered by robotic means? Why not let a human expedition bring back the goods?

Also speaking at MEPAG was Bruce Jakosky of the Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics at the University of Colorado Boulder and Department of Earth and Space Sciences at the University of Washington.

Jakosky called for an integrated approach to planning human missions to Mars. He highlighted recommendations stemming from a workshop in which he participated, held last May and organized by Explore Mars, Inc.
That report focused on the impact of MSR on reducing risk for human missions, rather than focusing on the science, Jakosky told Space.com.

"The purpose is to understand the risk to astronauts and to hardware. The risk includes that from compounds that are present in the soil that are hazardous to astronauts if breathed in," said Jakosky. "This includes perchlorates and chloromethanes that have been identified already, and detection of other species that might be present. It also includes dust that can be breathed in by astronauts and that can affect hardware wear and tear," he said.
During the MEPAG gathering, Jakosky flagged the importance of returning samples prior to human missions to Mars, such as:
- Identify and characterize known hazardous chemicals to ensure astronaut safety (e.g., perchlorates and chloromethanes), and look for possible additional hazardous chemicals
- Characterize very fine dust particles that could cause respiratory issues in astronauts
- Characterize dust and regolith properties for spacesuit design and wear patterns
- Search in advance of the arrival of humans for evidence of extant life that could interact with terrestrial life
- Enhance astronaut effectiveness on the surface and science return from human missions by providing initial context and analysis
- Demonstrate successful round-trip to Mars
- Demonstrate successful round-trip travel, including entry, descent, landing and ascent from the surface of Mars.

- Demonstrate implementation of planetary protection protocols. While human missions would not use the same approaches, what we learn from doing these would make the approach for humans much easier to plan and implement.
Yet one more forcing factor for NASA in yet another relook at MSR is that China is making progress on its Tianwen-3 Mars Sample Return mission.
According to the China National Space Administration, the country's Tianwen-3 probe will have a lander, an ascender, a service capsule, an orbiter, and an Earth reentry module.
Tianwen-3 appears on track getting the trek underway around 2028 on two Long March-5 heavy-lift carrier rockets from the Wenchang Space Launch Site in China's southernmost island province of Hainan.
China's Tianwen-3 mission is dedicated to bring back to Earth roughly 500 grams of Red Planet collectibles in 2031.

Leonard David is an award-winning space journalist who has been reporting on space activities for more than 50 years. Currently writing as Space.com's Space Insider Columnist among his other projects, Leonard has authored numerous books on space exploration, Mars missions and more, with his latest being "Moon Rush: The New Space Race" published in 2019 by National Geographic. He also wrote "Mars: Our Future on the Red Planet" released in 2016 by National Geographic. Leonard has served as a correspondent for SpaceNews, Scientific American and Aerospace America for the AIAA. He has received many awards, including the first Ordway Award for Sustained Excellence in Spaceflight History in 2015 at the AAS Wernher von Braun Memorial Symposium. You can find out Leonard's latest project at his website and on Twitter.

articles.title: SpaceX launches 2nd mystery mission for US Space Force in 6-day span (photos)
articles.author: Mike Wall

paras.en: SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force from California tonight (Nov. 11), the second such flight for the company in a six-day span.
A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:36 p.m. EST (8:36 p.m. local California time; 0136 GMT on Nov. 12), kicking off a mission called USSF-627.
Vandenberg hosted a similar liftoff less than a week ago: On Nov. 6, a Falcon 9 sent the USSF-432 mission skyward from the site, which lies on California's gorgeous but often foggy central coast.

We don't know much about USSF-627 or USSF-432; both are classified. Some experts have speculated, however, that each mission launched a batch of SpaceX's Starshield satellites for the Space Force's Space Based Sensing and Targeting portfolio, which helps the military branch track potential targets around the world.
SpaceX didn't reveal details about either USSF-627 or USSF-432, and the company ended the webcast of both launches shortly after the first stages of their Falcon 9 rockets came back to Earth.
In both cases, that touchdown occurred about 8.5 minutes after liftoff on the SpaceX droneship "Of Course I Still Love You," which was stationed downrange of Vandenberg in the Pacific Ocean.
It was the seventh mission for USSF-627's Falcon 9 booster, which carries the designation 1103.

USSF-627 was the 120th Falcon 9 launch of 2026 and the rocket's 15th national-security flight of the year to date. Eighty-five of the 120 flights have been devoted to building out SpaceX's Starlink broadband constellation in low Earth orbit, which currently consists of more than 11,000 satellites.
The Falcon 9 is not on a record-breaking cadence this year. In 2025, the rocket flew a whopping 165 missions, and 122 of them were Starlink flights.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

articles.title: Horizon Microtechnologies Targets Constellation-Scale Production As Esa Phi-Lab Selection Strengthens Industrialisation Push
articles.author: Horizon Microtechnologies

paras.en: (Karlsruhe, Germany, September 29th 2026) Horizon Microtechnologies is accelerating industrialisation of its metallised polymer micro-additive manufacturing platform through IP-MASS, a two-year scale-up project supported by €500,000 and reinforced by selection for ESA Phi-Lab Austria.

The programme is expanding Horizon’s printing, coating and process-verification capabilities for shielding housings and other passive RF hardware, targeting up to 50,000 precision-coated satellite components and a repeatable manufacturing framework suited to constellation-class demand rather than one-off prototype production.

Horizon combines precision polymer 3D printing with conformal metallisation and protective coatings. Polymer provides the precision bulk geometry, while metal is applied only to the thickness required. Replacing even lightweight metals such as aluminium with metallised polymer can reduce weight by 40%, while 3D printing can deliver further size, weight and design advantages alongside attractive economics compared with conventionally machined metal parts.

ESA Phi-Lab Austria’s “Industrialization by Design” focus supports upstream space technologies with commercial potential, reflecting the move towards scalable, reliable and cost-effective industrial products.

Importantly, IP-MASS is not limited to shielding housings. Horizon is also seeking spacecraft and space-related terrestrial applications where polymer 3D printing and metallisation could address product requirements, manufacturing constraints or future volume demand.

“Horizon has proved that metallised polymer micro-AM can deliver far more than lightweight prototypes,” said Andreas Frölich, CEO of Horizon Microtechnologies. “The next challenge is industrial: achieving the prices, lead times, repeatability and throughput needed when a component is required not once or ten times, but thousands or tens of thousands of times.”

Frölich adds, “Shielding housings give us a strong first industrialisation case, but they are not the limit. We also want to address components where lightweight printed geometry and functional metallic surfaces could create a meaningful technical or manufacturing advantage.”

The move builds on Horizon’s space-readiness work, which subjected representative metallised polymer demonstrators to established LEO tests including outgassing, temperature shock, radiation, mechanical shock, material fatigue and atomic-oxygen exposure.

For high-volume satellite architectures such as phased-array payloads, components may be used hundreds of times per spacecraft and across hundreds of satellites, turning component-level mass and cost savings into significant programme-level gains.

IP-MASS also provides scope to cooperate on applications with anticipated demand of 100 units per year or more. Partners do not need a fully developed component: early-stage concepts are welcome while design-for-manufacturability decisions can still be made.

“We do not want to assume that we already know every application where this technology can create value,” Frölich says. “The organisations designing next-generation spacecraft know where their product and manufacturing constraints are. We want them to bring those challenges to us so we can explore whether the technology is relevant and, where it is, potentially shape the manufacturing route together.”

Horizon is moving beyond validation towards an industrial manufacturing platform for next-generation satellite hardware, while inviting the space community to help identify which applications it should industrialise next.

Horizon is a member of the Green Space Center, an initiative supported by the State of Baden-Württemberg and based at the Chamber of Commerce and Industry Reutlingen (IHK Reutlingen) that promotes innovation in water management, New Space, and intelligent systems.

“We help SMEs in Baden-Württemberg internationalize space-related business models and products and support their entry into international markets,” said Marcin Bielecki, Head of Technology at the Green Space Center.

The initiative aims to position Baden-Württemberg as a sustainability-driven hub for space technology by fostering cross-sector collaboration and applying space technologies to create ecological impact.

Baden-Württemberg hosts a dynamic and rapidly growing New Space ecosystem, including leading European companies such as ATMOS Space Cargo, HyImpulse, ConstellR and CELERES while supporting emerging innovators such as InSpacePropulsion Technologies (ISPTech) and Yugen Space.

articles.title: Moog Marks 25 Years Since ESPA Design Milestone: Innovating Space Rideshare
articles.author: Moog Inc.

paras.en: East Aurora, N.Y. — Moog Inc. (NYSE: MOG.A and MOG.B) marks 25 years since the Evolved Secondary Payload Adapter (ESPA) ring completed its Critical Design Review in 2001. The pioneering technology helped advance space rideshare by enabling multiple payloads to share a launch and broadening access to orbit for commercial, government, and defense missions.

Development of ESPA began in 1999 through a collaborative government-industry initiative, culminating in the successful completion of its Critical Design Review on January 18, 2001. The ESPA ring enabled launch vehicles to carry multiple secondary payloads by efficiently using previously unused volume beneath primary satellites. This approach lowered costs and increased mission flexibility, supporting commercial satellite constellations, technology demonstrations, and critical defense operations.

paras.en: “ESPA helped redefine access to space by enabling additional payloads to share a launch with primary missions. Its impact continues across commercial, government, and military space—and its story reflects the value of enduring collaboration between Air Force Research Lab (AFRL) and industry partners such as Moog,” said Dr. Darren Raspa, chief historian, AFRL Space and Directed Energy Systems.

Over the past 25 years, the ESPA family has evolved into a versatile, modular platform supporting varied payload sizes and interface configurations. ESPA-derived designs have also served as the structural foundation for spacecraft buses. Today, the platform continues to support mission planning for NASA, the U.S. government, and commercial space ventures worldwide.

Moog continues to offer a family of ESPA configurations, including Standard ESPA, ESPA Heavy, and ESPA Grande, designed to accommodate evolving payload and mission requirements. The platform’s modular architecture and adaptable interfaces support rideshare missions, payload integration, and spacecraft applications across the growing space market.

“The ESPA ring began as a technical solution to a practical challenge: maximizing every launch opportunity,” said Timothy Pargett, general manager, Moog Payload Adapters and Isolation business. “Today, it stands as a cornerstone of how missions, large and small, gain cost-effective, reliable access to orbit through rideshare. Its enduring legacy reflects visionary innovation and trusted partnerships across the aerospace community.”

In conjunction with the anniversary, a Moog flight-qualified ESPA ring will be on display at the National Museum of Nuclear Science & History in Albuquerque, N.M., from November 7, 2026, through January 10, 2027.
Museum visitors will have the opportunity to see firsthand the hardware that helped advance rideshare and enable diverse space missions.

As ESPA enters its next chapter, Moog continues to advance spacecraft payload integration and develop adaptable solutions that expand flexible, cost-effective access to orbit for future space exploration and defense missions.

Moog is a worldwide designer, manufacturer, and systems integrator of high-performance precision motion and fluid controls and control systems. Moog’s high-performance systems control military and commercial aircraft, satellites, and space vehicles, launch vehicles, defense systems, missiles, automated industrial machinery, marine, and medical equipment. Additional information about the Company can be found at www.moog.com or www.moog.com/space.

articles.title: Senate committee takes up nominees for NASA chief financial officer and inspector general
articles.author: Jeff Foust

paras.en: WASHINGTON — A Senate committee is set to advance nominations for NASA’s chief financial officer and inspector general.

The Senate Commerce Committee held a hearing Nov. 10 to consider nominations for several posts, including that of Joshua Shoemaker to be NASA’s chief financial officer and Robert Steinau to be inspector general. Those are two of the four positions at the agency that require Senate confirmation; the others are administrator and deputy administrator.

Neither nominee received many questions during the hearing, which lasted a little more than an hour. Senators largely focused their attention on the nomination of Danielle Thumann to be a member of the Federal Communications Commission.

Shoemaker is an accountant who has worked for more than 20 years in the private sector and in the Mississippi state government. Since August, he has been a senior adviser in NASA’s Mission Support Directorate, and before that was controller for the Republican National Committee.

Steinau has worked since 2009 at NASA’s Office of Inspector General, and since December 2024 has served as the office’s senior official in the absence of a Senate-confirmed inspector general. He previously worked for the Department of Energy’s Office of Inspector General and for the U.S. Secret Service.

Shoemaker, in his opening statement at the nomination hearing, said he would focus on financial accountability, improved visibility into financial performance of NASA programs, transparency with Congress on that performance and modernization of NASA financial systems.

“I believe the CFO has an important responsibility to give the administrator, NASA leadership and Congress an honest and timely picture of the agency’s financial position,” he said. He added that means how programs are performing against their planned budgets and schedules as well as ensuring effective management of resources.

He deferred questions on specific programs as well as on the proposed U.S. Space Academy that a presidential commission, led by NASA, is studying. Shoemaker said that decisions on locating the academy will ultimately be made by the president.

Steinau said that, as inspector general, he would focus on three critical challenges for NASA: returning humans to the moon, transitioning from the International Space Station to commercial stations and cybersecurity.
“NASA is moving with urgency, and it is imperative that accountability keep pace with ambition,” he said.
The Senate Commerce Committee announced Nov. 11 that it will meet Nov. 18 to vote on the nominees at the Nov. 10 hearing, sending them, if approved, to the full Senate for a confirmation vote.

NASA has been without a Senate-confirmed chief financial officer since the start of the Trump administration in January 2025. The White House nominated Greg Autry for that position in the spring of 2025, but the nomination was returned by the Senate without acting on it at the end of the year. NASA has lacked a Senate-confirmed inspector general since the departure of Paul Martin in late 2023.

articles.title: Curiosity Blog, Sols 5063-5069 Rocks and Chips

paras.en: Written by William Farrand, Senior Research Scientist, Space Science Institute
Earth planning date: Friday, Nov. 6, 2026

This week Curiosity has been completing its drill campaign at the “Nazca” drill hole. This is an area characterized by bedrock containing disk-shaped (or in a liberal interpretation, potato chip shaped … see linked image) crystal forms. A key objective has been to better characterize these chip-shaped features. Drill samples were delivered to the Sample Analysis for Mars (SAM) instrument. While the SAM analysis was on-going, Monday’s plan included a ChemCam LIBS observation of another crystal-form, “Ahi Veremos,” more Mastcam frames to fill out a mosaic of the Nazca near to mid-field, and environmental observations including a large dust devil survey, and horizon and atmospheric zenith movies.

articles.title: Scotland’s Flow Country

paras.en: Compared to ecosystems in many other parts of the world, the blanket bogs of the Flow Country in northern Scotland are unassuming—soggy, treeless landscapes dominated by hummocky mosses, grasses, and heathers. Yet, to ecologists, the seemingly desolate areas are nothing short of extraordinary.

The bogs store tremendous quantities of carbon. That’s because their soils are so waterlogged that microbes cannot fully break down dead plant material, a process that would otherwise release carbon dioxide. Instead, partially decayed plant matter accumulates into thick layers of spongy, crumbly, carbon-rich material called peat.

The unusual ecosystems, also called blanket mires and featherbed bogs, only occur in places with abundant rainfall, poor drainage, and low levels of evapotranspiration. These types of bogs cover just 120,000 square kilometers (46,000 square miles) globally, less than one-tenth of one percent of Earth’s land surface. The image above, captured by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 8, is centered on blanket bogs in the Scottish Highlands, home to the largest such ecosystem in Europe. This peatland is also the first of its type to be inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The peat bogs of northern Scotland, home to more than 30 species of sphagnum moss, are spread across some 1,900 square kilometers (730 square miles) of the country’s Highlands region. In this image, boggy areas appear dark brown and are sprinkled with lakes. The light green area on the right side around Thurso is farmland. The darker green geometric patterns in the center are conifer plantations. The image was captured in the spring, the part of the year when the land surface is most waterlogged and peat bogs begin to accumulate large amounts of new biomass.

paras.en: While forests store most of their carbon in living trees—which eventually release it back into the atmosphere when they burn or die—peat bogs often store carbon for many thousands of years. Some parts of the Flow Country have been accumulating peat for more than 9,000 years, building deposits exceeding eight meters thick, according to UNESCO. Overall, scientists estimate that all of the world’s peatlands cover just 3 percent of Earth’s land surface but store more than 600 gigatons of carbon—about twice as much as all the world’s forests combined.

articles.title: Sudan war: First ‘suicide’ drone attacks, now long-range strikes are the norm

paras.en: Sudan war: First ‘suicide’ drone attacks, now long-range strikes are the norm

Drones and drought are “closing in” on Sudan, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF), said on Tuesday, describing unprecedented attacks on the country’s infrastructure including by drones travelling up to 1,500 kilometres before hitting their target.

“It is an assault unlike anything Sudan has seen before. In the last week of October, not a single day passed without a drone strike on a power station in Sudan. Up to 15 were hit in the month of October,” said agency spokesperson James Elder.

“This year in Sudan, two in three child casualties were killed by armed drones. They are bringing war to places that were once safe. People in Sudan talk about three things: they talk about safety, education and water. Drones are taking all three.”
The UNICEF alert comes amid ongoing fighting between former allies turned military rivals the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).

Well over 15 million people urgently require shelter across the country but drone strikes on civilians, markets and key public infrastructure continue to hinder aid efforts and increase the suffering of non-combatants.
“Several years ago, there was a use of suicide drones, which was terrifying to see that in Sudan,” Mr. Elder explained.

Highlighting the use of increasingly accurate long-range drones in the last 12 months, including some travelling 1,500 kilometres, he explained that it was impossible for humanitarian agencies like UNICEF to ascertain who was behind “at least 15 strikes” on Sudanese power stations in October. “One would struggle to think if it was in the interest of the SAF, of Government, to do that,” he added.

Straight off the plane from Sudan, Mr. Elder told journalists in Geneva about one of the many young war victims he had met from El Obeid, where UN Human Rights Council investigators say that civilians live in constant fear of drone attack.

“Buri is a teenager. An explosive took both his hands. He lives in a tent. He told me, ‘I must accept this,’” Mr. Elder explained. “He spends the mornings learning online and the afternoons picking grass for animals with stumps for hands. His friends help him, that’s Sudan. It’s relentless. It’s crushing.”

Like Ukraine, Sudan’s energy sector is being struck repeatedly, but unlike in Ukraine, Sudanese targets are not repaired, the UNICEF spokesperson stressed: “When a power station is struck, water pumps stop, water treatment stops. Families are forced into expensive and unsafe alternatives.”
Harvests suffer, prices keep rising and food slips further and further out of reach
In addition, disease is spreading, the agency warns, with pockets of cholera identified and the cold chain for vaccines and medicines increasingly threatened by the ongoing war.
Farmers are also losing the ability to irrigate crops because their pumps run on electricity generators which are too expensive to operate because of “crippling” fuel shortages, Mr. Elder continued.

“Harvests suffer, prices keep rising and food slips further and further out of reach: a lethal cycle kicks in…All this at a time when an estimated 825,000 children under five in Sudan are expected to suffer from severe acute malnutrition this year; the type that kills.”
As part of the wider UN response, UNICEF and partners have treated hundreds of thousands of children for the deadliest form of malnutrition.

The agency has provided healthcare to more than 2.5 million people and vaccinated millions of children against deadly diseases. Teams have also repaired and hooked up water systems to solar power, helping to keep safe water flowing for close to eight million people.

But with “so many crises happening at once, everything, everything is at breaking point”, Mr. Elder said, noting that UNICEF’s response in Sudan is just one-third funded. “Resilience cannot run on goodwill alone,” he insisted.

articles.title: From Japan to Rwanda, early warnings are saving lives – but millions remain unprotected

paras.en: From Japan to Rwanda, early warnings are saving lives – but millions remain unprotected

Early warning systems are saving lives across the globe, but for millions of people the warning never arrives, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said on Wednesday, urging the world to protect every person on Earth by the end of 2027.

“No one should lose their life simply because a warning came too late – or never came at all,” he told a high-level event on the Early Warnings for All initiative at the COP31 climate conference, which runs until 20 November in Antalya, Türkiye.

His appeal came as a new report from the UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) showed that 136 countries – 70 per cent of the total – now report having multi-hazard early warning systems, 17 more than in March 2025.
Yet major gaps remain in the most vulnerable countries, as a powerful El Niño raises the stakes.

The report, Global Status of Multi-Hazard Early Warning Systems 2026, finds that countries with substantial to comprehensive systems record disaster-related mortality 6.1 times lower than those with limited to moderate ones, and 3.2 times fewer people affected.

It also shows what that means on the ground. When a magnitude 8.8 earthquake struck off Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula in July 2025, the Pacific Tsunami Warning Center issued its first threat messages within 10 minutes.

Japan evacuated approximately 1.9 million people, while in Ecuador’s Galápagos islands, more than 2,300 people were moved out of high-risk areas hours before waves of about 1.3 metres reached the shore.

In Madagascar, an early action plan developed by the Malagasy Red Cross was partially activated before Tropical Cyclone Gezani made landfall in February, with some 600 door-to-door visits reaching 80,000 to 100,000 people with warnings and evacuation support.

And in Rwanda’s Karongi district, a tea farmer and her daughters were warned – through women’s cooperatives, SMS, local radio and loudspeakers – that heavy rain was expected within 48 hours, giving her time to reinforce her terraces, clear water channels and store her dried tea leaves before the downpour.

Around one in three countries still has no early warning system, Mr. Guterres said, with the widest gaps in least developed countries, small island developing States and countries affected by conflict.
“They did the least to cause the climate crisis, but are being hit first and hardest,” he said.
“Some European countries have more weather stations that meet global standards than the entire continent of Africa,” the Secretary-General added. “We cannot warn people about what we cannot see.”
WMO chief Celeste Saulo warned that the current El Niño “could be literally off our monitoring charts”.
“While we cannot stop El Niño, we can prevent many of its worst human consequences,” she said.
Urging countries to “accelerate and build systems that last”, Mr. Guterres set out three priorities:
- making early warnings a permanent public service;
- closing financing and capacity gaps; and
- moving from fragmented projects to coordinated, long-term support for country-led plans.

Since 2022, some $2 billion has been mobilised and around 160 countries are receiving support, he noted. But finance must cover the entire warning chain, he said; “from weather forecasting to communication tools to volunteers knocking on doors”.
Warnings are also increasingly triggering action before disaster strikes: in 2025, 146 anticipatory action activations in 54 countries reached 9.6 million people, the report found.
“Countries have made significant progress in strengthening their early warning systems, but too many people remain unprotected,” said Kamal Kishore, head of UNDRR.
“The climate crisis is accelerating. Our protection of people must accelerate with it,” Mr. Guterres said. “Together, let us make sure that every warning arrives in time.”

articles.title: Gaza winter aid: ‘No more delay’, Fletcher tells governments stalling on support

paras.en: Gaza winter aid: ‘No more delay’, Fletcher tells governments stalling on support

The UN’s Emergency Relief Coordinator, Tom Fletcher, expressed deep concern about the deteriorating humanitarian situation in Gaza, as UN member states and partners have been repeatedly delaying sending their support to the Strip.

“Foreign Ministers and partners have assured me of support, but also repeatedly said that progress would be hard until after Israeli elections. Now we’re told to wait for the formation of a Government,” he said.
“In case anyone has any doubt about international humanitarian law: this is not an acceptable excuse, as the international community and Board of Peace have made clear,” Mr. Fletcher stressed.
With winter underway, people living in Gaza are facing ever-harsher living conditions, including freezing temperatures and harsh storms which collapse or flood the tents thousands are living in.

“What makes this even more infuriating is that they are at this needless risk from weather that is not a threat where decent shelter exists. And would not be such a threat had we been able to supply decent tents and essential Winter kit,” Mr. Fletcher said.
The UN relief chief stressed that the UN had a “clear plan” for which supplies need to reach Gaza, “not in weeks, but weeks ago,” with each delay costing lives.

The list includes durable shelter, warm clothes, blankets, bedding and safe heating solutions, as well as generators, fuel, engine oil, spare parts, equipment to pump out water, remove debris and clear explosive ordnance.

“No more delay. Open all the crossings, not just one. Let our vital NGO partners work. Allow the commercial markets to function. Stop this collective punishment. Fund the plan. End this predictable, preventable suffering,” he urged.

The UN’s labour agency (ILO) on Wednesday, called on international partners to increase their financial support for a jobs-led recovery plan in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (OPT), which aims to lay the conditions for long-term resilience and stability.

“Humanitarian assistance alone cannot restore livelihoods, essential services, or the institutional foundations needed for sustainable recovery,” said Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator, Ramiz Alakbarov.

In Gaza alone, 252,000 jobs were lost between the third quarters of 2023 and 2025, unemployment reached a staggering 85.1 per cent and labour income losses totalled $2.77 billion, with women and young people facing particularly limited prospects.
“Behind every job lost is a person, a family and a future placed at risk,” said ILO Director-General Gilbert F. Houngbo.
The ILO’s Decent Work and Recovery Programme (DWRP) supports emergency employment, enterprise recovery, social protection and stronger labour institutions to address the issue.
Over the past three years, it has helped generate approximately 130,000 paid workdays and contributed to social allowances reaching over 30,000 older persons and persons with disabilities.

articles.title: Age-old rivalry bookends RLWC but will it end 18 years of supremacy?

paras.en: Australia vs New Zealand: Age-old rivalry bookends Rugby League World Cup but will it end 18 years of supremacy?

In the men's and women's Rugby League World Cup finals Australia will take on New Zealand; the last time both New Zealand teams won the tournament was back in 2008, nearly two decades ago; the finals take place on Sunday November 16

An age-old rivalry will bookend the Rugby League World Cup 2026 in the latest symbol that rugby league worldwide has grown but, ultimately, the contenders are still just contenders and the favourites remain just that.
In a sensational opener to the tournament, Australia clinched a dramatic 24-22 victory over New Zealand in front of the biggest Test crowd in 50 years, surpassing the previous benchmark set in 1974.
Now, the two men's teams will meet once again to decide who will be world champions. And in the women's tournament, the same showdown will decide who is on top.

Australia and New Zealand have contested the last four women's World Cup finals. In the men's, Australia have cemented their spot as ever with New Zealand returning to the final for the first time since 2013.

New Zealand's men's side have won the World Cup just once back in 2008. The women's side have won it on three occasions but not in 18 years, their last glory coming back in 2008 - the last year New Zealand were on top of the world.
Since then, it has been total and utter Australian domination. New Zealand Women head into their fifth final in a row against the Jillaroos. They do not want it to be a fifth loss in a row.

Coming into this Rugby League World Cup, the talk was all about the new contenders, the ones that had been growing and growing and looked like, this time, they could take down the big boys. The talk was all about Tonga and Samoa showing the landscape of rugby league internationally had changed.
Throughout the group stage, they looked primed and their showdown in the final pool round, in which Tonga came away 20-18 victors, seemed to be the marker that they were here for the big win.
In the end, that match between the two nations ultimately became their final of sorts.
Following that, Tonga succumbed to New Zealand and Samoa fell short of Australia in the men's semi-finals. Exciting Samoa Women could not keep up in a 32-0 loss to New Zealand Women.
They edged closer in some respects but could not complete the job.
The task is set for New Zealand's men - do what they did 18 years ago and release Australia's near two-decade long grip on the title.

Kalyn Ponga became the emblem of how the change to State of Origin eligibility would open up the international landscape as he could still play for Queensland but also represent his heritage. He did that valiantly by returning from a broken arm in that opening clash within just 22 days to star in the semi-finals.
What it would mean to him to complete the journey.
The World Cup storyline, for many, was going to be how a nation could defy the odds to win and send shockwaves globally.
While on the face of it New Zealand winning seems normal, it is anything but. They can still change the landscape, mark their moment, move the competition on.
A victory for them means Australia will be denied the chance to say they have been world champions for 20 years - surely that is as good a motivation as any?
One bookend is a win for Australia. Could the other bookend be glory for New Zealand?

articles.title: Cummins to address Khawaja 'Sandpapergate' claims on Friday

paras.en: 'Sandpapergate': Australia captain Pat Cummins to address Usman Khawaja claims on Friday

Usman Khawaja says in new book 'Sabr' that every Australia player was aware of ball-tampering scheme in Cape Town in 2018; current Test captain Pat Cummins confirms he's "happy to speak with any and all media" on Friday; white-ball skipper for England series Mitch Marsh declined to comment

Australia captain Pat Cummins has called a press conference for Friday to have his say on 'Sandpapergate' after former team-mate Usman Khawaja's explosive claims that the entire dressing room knew about the ball-tampering scheme that took place on the tour of South Africa in 2018.
Khawaja made the revelations in his new book 'Sabr', bringing the scandal back onto the agenda after eight years.
Cummins has been rested for the white-ball series' against England, which also begins on Friday with the first ODI in Perth, but has publicly invited a media grilling in Sydney for that same morning.

"I'm training at Cricket Central (in Sydney) tomorrow morning before the Blues play in the Shield match," Cummins posted on X on Thursday. "Happy to speak with any and all media about the events of this week at 9.30 am.
"I've taken some time to try and better understand the long list and full extent of Uzzy's allegations so I can respond properly."

In the immediate aftermath of the Cape Town Test in 2018, in which Cameron Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball, only he, then captain Steve Smith and David Warner - who said on Monday that Khawaja's version of events was "100 per cent accurate" - were banned.

Khawaja's revelations have invited renewed speculation over the role of the bowling group who benefitted from the ball manipulation - with Cummins, Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon having previously distanced themselves from the episode.

In 2021, the quartet issued a carefully worded statement responding to "rumour mongering and innuendo" in which they denied knowing that a foreign substance had been taken onto the field to alter the ball in order to try and make it swing.
Cricket Australia chairman David Boon has backed Cummins, saying his job as skipper is not under threat.

"We absolutely support Pat," Boon said in comments published by The Australian on Thursday. "He's been an exemplary captain, he's led the team with integrity and, you know, very successfully over the period of time that he's been captain, so there's no question of our confidence in him continuing on in that fact."

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, after Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg insisted there would be no re-opening of the 'Sandpapergate' investigation, Starc said of Khawaja's claims: "I haven't really paid much attention to it to be fair.
"There are differing opinions of eight years ago. We were heavily grilled through the process, at the time and since.
"I won't speak on behalf of the bowlers but from where I stand my opinion hasn't changed, my recollection hasn't changed from what we said in 2021.
"As far as our statement said, we weren't aware of things being taken on the field. That's where I'll leave it.
"I will be sticking to what I said five years ago, what I said at the time eight years ago, so clearly there are differing versions from different people.
"We weren't aware of anything taken on the field to be tampered with. We saw it on the big screen in Cape Town.
"As far as the book is concerned, I haven't read it. I probably won't read it, so that's for Usman to elaborate on."
On Khawaja saying the ball was also tampered with in the Test before the Cape Town fixture, at Port Elizabeth, now Gqeberha, Starc added: "That's the first I was aware of any of that."
Starc, Cummins, Hazlewood and Lyon are not part of the upcoming white-ball series at home to England.
Marsh not drawn on Khawaja claims | Root: It's all speculation

Captain of Australia for the three-match ODI series and five T20s against England, Mitchell Marsh - who was in the Test team that toured South Africa in 2018 - declined to comment at a press conference in Perth on Thursday.
"I respect (Khawaja) for telling his story and for writing his book, and I don't sit here coming from a place of judgment on any of that," Marsh said ahead of Friday's series-opening ODI.
"It was a really tough time for Australian cricket. There's still a lot of people hurting. Now is not the time for me to share my story.
"My honest answer is because I've personally moved on. I respect that others probably haven't, but I have. And I hope that's respected."

He added: "Everyone's got their story. Some will be willing to share it, and others might not, purely on the basis of the fact that they've moved on. I think it's really important that at some stage we do."
In his book, Khawaja also said Australia experimented with lifting the seam on the ball during the 2017-18 Ashes at home to England, which they won 4-0 under the captaincy of Smith.
The ECB said 'no comment' when approached by Sky Sports News.
"It's all speculation. I wasn't in that dressing room. I don't know what went on. I don't want to speculate, as I said. My focus is with this (ODI) team right now and what we've got coming up."
Cricket Australia: No compelling reason to re-open 'Sandpapergate' case

A statement from the Australian Cricketers' Association called the 2018 scandal a "low point for Australian cricket" for which Smith, Warner and Bancroft paid an "enormous" and "disproportionate" price.

The statement added: "There are no winners in this issue, and nothing can undo what happened. There are humans in the centre of this and we will be calling for the ongoing vitriol directed at those involved to come to an end."

Greenberg, who was not part of Cricket Australia at the time of the scandal, told Australian radio station SEN on the decision not to launch a fresh inquiry: "We don't see any compelling reason to open the investigation or revisit this again.
"I don't think there's anything that can be gained from that.
"We have said we're comfortable with the outcome of the investigation based on the information we've received. That includes what we've seen from Usman. Our position hasn't changed on that.

"There's absolutely no benefit in going back, that's the clear position of the CA board. I think it's fine, we've got to look ahead, and the matter was dealt with under a previous leadership back in 2018.
"Trying to second-guess decisions from a previous time or making an assessment through the prism of hindsight is not something we want to do."
'Usman's version of events inconsistent with what others say'
The Cricket Australia CEO added: "When you cut to the core of the challenge that we face here, Usman's version of events is inconsistent with what others have had to say.
"I can assure you there are lots of other players who have a very, very different version of events and they have made that very public from the very start of 2018.
"They have been very consistent in their position right through until today. From my conversations with many over the weekend, I don't think that will change either.
"I think we end up at the same intersection point, which is that eight years ago people have a version of events which differ from each other.
"No one would like to get this chapter of Australian cricket closed more than me, but it is unlikely."

Former Australia captain Michael Clarke hopes the truth comes to light, saying that chance was missed in the wake of the scandal in 2018 and then again three years later when Bancroft replied it was "probably self-explanatory" after being asked whether the bowling attack knew of the sandpaper use.

Clarke told 2DayFM: "[Australia fans] can't trust what's real. They don't know the truth until this gets reopened and the truth comes out. I would just like to see whatever the truth is for it all to come out, allow people to move on.

"For me, right now, there are more questions than answers. I want to know, firstly, did everyone know? Because certain players have come out and said they didn't. That's important information so we can get the truth.
"I can't believe we haven't heard from Cummins yet. Steve Smith lost his job. If this doesn't happen, Tim Paine never captains Australia. And neither does Cummins.
"Cummins would not have captained a game at this stage if 'Sandpapergate' didn't happen because Smith would still be captain."

articles.title: Darts star Sheldon on brilliant Beau and the Littler effect hitting Ireland

paras.en: Darts player Katie Sheldon: Irish ace on brilliant Beau Greaves and how Littler Littler has inspired a boom in Ireland

Katie Sheldon talks about Beau Greaves and how Littler Littler is inspiring the next generation of players in Ireland; 'Beau 'n' Arrow' faces Littler at the Grand Slam of Darts; you can watch the tournament in Wolverhampton live on Sky Sports from November 14-22
Katie Sheldon - nicknamed 'The Dublin Diamond' - is a pioneer of women's darts in Ireland at the tender age of 22.
As one of the hottest prospects to come out of the Emerald Isle, Sheldon has already competed on the Women's Series and at the Women's World Matchplay held at the iconic Winter Gardens in Blackpool.
Currently working as a wire assembler, Sheldon has already become the World Masters girls' champion and a two-time WDF World Cup team winner.

"I keep saying that one goal of mine is to pick up a PDC title, so a Women's Series. And along with that, it's trying to qualify for the Women's World Matchplay," she told Sky Sports, having taken part in the Netflix 'Beat Luke Littler' challenge in which she was given the chance to win £501,000.

It wasn't to be for Sheldon over one leg against 'The Nuke', but she has bigger dreams of emulating brilliant Beau Greaves, who finished a dominant season on the PDC Women's Series by winning 17 out of 24 events.

The Doncaster thrower will be at the Grand Slam of Darts where she has been drawn with Luke Littler and Niels Zonneveld. She also secured her qualification for the world championship at Alexandra Palace alongside 'Beat Luke Littler' winner Fallon Sherrock, Gemma Hayter, 'The Lancashire Rose' Lisa Ashton, and Belgian-born Swedish darts player, Vicky Pruim.

'Beau 'n' Arrow' made history in April by becoming the first woman to win a PDC ranking title at Players Championship 11 in Milton Keynes, defeating three former world champions, Rob Cross, Gary Anderson and Michael Smith.

She has risen to 75th in the PDC Order of Merit with the youngster closing in on the world's top 64, an achievement that would have ramifications for her future in the Women's Series with female players who break into the top 64 globally and hold a Tour Card restricted from playing in the Women's Series.
"She's really a great talent, and she's pushed us all," said Sheldon. "I think her being there has actually brought the standard up.
"Her being there has been a massive help to all of the women to progress their game, but I think it would be a sad loss to the Women's Series when she's gone."
The success of two-time back-to-back world champion Littler has played a huge part in the surge of youth academies - not least in Ireland where Sheldon has seen a surge in interest.
She explained: "I think Luke has given everyone that [interest]. I think a lot of people have started picking up darts, but mainly youths.
"When I played youth darts in youth academies, there wasn't that many of us, a couple of lads, but the numbers are just through the roof now.
"We have a Dublin academy, and I think at the team event, there was 183 kids there at the weekend, just playing darts for their local teams and clubs, which is amazing for the sport.
"It's great to see the growth, and I think a lot of that is down to what Luke's done."
'People probably don't know what they're witnessing'
Despite his success, Littler has threatened to boycott certain tournaments after being booed and whistled by vociferous crowds - not least in the Netherlands and Germany.
Sheldon accepts "it's a hard one to take" for players as well as Littler, himself.
She said: "When he first came on the scene, everyone was bigging him up and it was great, but then you're turning up to tournaments and people are booing him.
"People probably don't know what they're witnessing at the minute. The standard of darts is just crazy.

"I think if you are a fan, you should be going there to enjoy it. Don't get me wrong, everyone loves singing the songs, but I think there should be just that level of respect for the players when they're playing because at the end of the day, this is their livelihood as well.
"They want to be trying to perform the best for the fans, and they probably can't do that with all the boos.
"It's one of those things he has to deal with, which is kind of sad to see."
